documents.title: Development of Artificial Reefs Using Environmentally Safe Ceramic Material
documents.snippet:
The development of artificial fish reefs has been studied worldwide to enhance fish abundance and diversity, recover coastal and marine habitats, and restore damaged coral reefs [1][2][3][4][5]. Various materials have been used in the construction of artificial reefs worldwide. They include bamboo, concrete blocks, ceramic structures, fibre glass, pipes, reinforced plastic, metal, and marine alloys [6]. Every material, however, has some drawbacks when used as artificial reefs. Bamboo and wood are easily scattered by water currents, lose their fish-aggregating integrity, and cause further degradation of the sea bed [7]. Concrete blocks are durable and can be structured in various configurations, but have limited applications because of their cost [7]. In fact, placing any type of material in the marine environment poses a risk of causing pollution, which would have harmful effects on marine ecosystems [7]. Therefore, by considering detrimental effects apart from benefits, it is necessary to choose materials that have minimal negative impacts on marine environments and can enhance fish colonization. In this regard, ceramic materials are one of the best candidates, because they are economical, environmentally safe, and suitable for hostile marine environments. Santos et al. [8] studied the fish colonization of artificial reefs made of ceramic, concrete, and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) pipes, and they found that ceramic reefs were more effectively colonized than concrete and PVC reefs. Although there have been some studies on the colonization of fish in ceramic reefs, few studies have shown effective reef design and functionality of ceramic materials in a shallow sea environment. 

In this research, ceramic artificial reefs with a hexagonal column structure were designed from a ceramic material. They would be set on sandy sea beds to obtain hard and flat sea beds. The effectiveness of the hexagonal structure was investigated by determining the mechanical strength of the reefs and their sustainability in an adverse shallow sea environment. Ceramic materials were analyzed by measuring chemical constituents, surface texture, water absorption, erosion rate, and durability. These qualities were compared with those of natural coral rubbles.

Title: Enhancing reef fish diversity using artificial reef-building: A case study of coral reef rehabilitation on Nyamuk Island, Anambas Islands
Snippet: The establishment of the module as a transplanting medium used a mixture of cement and sand, which then formed into an effective and efficient shape for Anambas water conditions. These coral transplantation modules were built like a furnace to increase effectiveness when the modules were being deployed.

Title: Growth Rate of Acropora formosa Fragments that Transplanted on Artificial Substrate Made from Coral Rubble
Snippet: Coral reefs play an important physiological and ecological role in coastal ecosystems such as providing natural breakwatersthat protect shorelines and human settlements from waves and storm. Corals killed by tsunami, waves and storms are often degraded into rubble. This rubble is dynamic, easily shifted by currents and storms, which effectively forms â€˜â€˜killing fieldsâ€™â€™ forcoral juveniles, hindering coral recovery. In order to rehabilitate coral reefs, artificial substrates are used both for coral transplantation and recruitment. Unfortunately, most artificial substrates are expensive and use land-based material such asconcrete/cement-bases. In order to develop a new low-cost artificial substrate that can replace concrete/cement-base as amedia for coral transplantation, modified coral rubble was tested in a pilot study in Seribu Island, Jakarta. Two different nets (nylon and polyethylene) were used to form rubble into a compact shape, stable and strong substrate. The stability of therubble and the complexity of the surface which is created by the net make this substrate suitable for coral transplantation.Additionally, from an economic perspective the nets are very cheap and locally available. In a number of experiments,modified coral rubble successfully replaced the concrete /cement-base as a media for coral transplantation. The coral transplants were growing over time. With this method, we can try to rehabilitate the degraded coral reef destroyed by tsunami or other factors with material that already is available at the site and with less money. However, this approach requires testing at additional sites and for longer periods, to determine the replicability of the results.Key words: cement base, coral, rubble, transplantation

Title: Assembled concrete reefs as a stand for coral transplantation on the seabed
Snippet: Reefs are also known as a ridge of jagged rock below the surface of the sea, which are places where coral attaches [1], so reefs that are overgrown with coral are called coral reefs which are one of the ecosystems in the sea [2]. This Assembled Concrete Reefs [4] is designed to be resistant to the conditions of the monsoon season sea waters. 

The concrete material as patented artificial coral [5] forms from a single artificial coral concrete in the form of a tetrapod form [6,7], a structure with a spatial shape [8] and a semicircle [9] exists, then an artificial reef with blocks that can be combined [10], then from the combined polyethylene pipe [11] and the combined coconut shell [12].This research goal is to design the artificial reef that can be efficiently assembled and function effectively.

Title: Coral transplantation on a multilevel substrate of Artificial Patch Reefs: effect of fixing methods on the growth rate of two Acropora species
Snippet: Coral reef is one of an important ecosystem on earth, it is most complex and biodiverse ecosystem that provides the ecological services for humankind. Recently, coral reefs worldwide have been degrading by natural and manmade stress (Wilkinson 2000;Burke et al. 2011). Reef health has been declining apparently by limiting space for natural recruitment and change in physical environmental conditions (Done et al. 2010). Thus, coral reef rehabilitation is considered one of the major reef management strategies that coral reefs may not be able to recover naturally without human intervention. 

To rehabilitate damage of natural reefs, artificial reefs and coral transplantation has been applied regardless of environmental condition, cause of decline, or goals. Coral transplantation generally applied by transplanted coral fragments on table cages in shallow water in order to cultivate coral fragments due to transferred and transplanted to rehabilitation reef areas (Heeger and Sotto 2000;Ammar 2013). It seems to be the most widely implemented for coral reef rehabilitation. Many studies dealing with reef rehabilitation by applied coral transplantation (Yap 2000(Yap , 2004;;Epstein et al. 2001Epstein et al. , 2003;;Sabater and Yap 2002). Coral transplantation may contribute to enhance the coral population in the reef areas, although natural recovery indicated by coral recruitment (Edwards and Clark 1998;Ng et al. 2015). Coral transplantation method potentially has an impact on reef health by losing colonies from the donor area, reducing the growth of transplanted corals, reducing fecundity of transplant due to stress. Alternatively, artificial reefs are considered an efficient rehabilitation tool, it is a suitable method for protection of existing natural reefs, environmental, mitigation for damaged reef areas and shoreline protections (Meester et al. 2015;Ng et al. 2016). Artificial reefs are expected to increase in available substrates for reef organisms, provide structural complexity and natural recruitment. However, the application of these methods in Indonesia waters was apparently not successful, indicated by high mortality of coral fragments in coral transplantation and many artificial reefs that applied damage to natural reefs (Munasik 2009). In order to optimize reef rehabilitation, combining artificial reefs and coral transplantation is recommended (Abelson 2006;Ammar et al. 2013;Cummings et al. 2015).

Title: Coral transplantation on a multilevel substrate of Artificial Patch Reefs: effect of fixing methods on the growth rate of two Acropora species
Snippet: In order to optimize reef rehabilitation, combining artificial reefs and coral transplantation is recommended (Abelson 2006;Ammar et al. 2013;Cummings et al. 2015). 

Artificial Patch Reefs (APR) is an artificial structure which is applied to rehabilitate coral reef in order to develop shallow water habitat (Munasik et al. 2018). APR is a rehabilitation tool that is designed by multilevel substrates and applied the combination both of coral transplantation and artificial reefs. Acropora spp. is generally considered as a good for candidates for use in coral transplantation or population enhancement project due to their high growth rate and high survivorship of fragments (Lirman et al. 2010;Boch and Morse 2012;Mercado-Molina 2016;Schopmeyer et al. 2017). The application of APR with Acropora transplanted on their substrates is considered contributing to the local conservation of the small island reefs in the near future. In this study, two Acropora species were selected and applied to investigate the suitable method and species selection for reef rehabilitation. Multilevel substrates of APR may provide the hard substrate to facilitate fragment of coral grows in shallow turbid water. However, the information about the effect of multilevel substrates on survival and growth of transplanted corals is limited. This study aims to address the effectiveness of the APR structure to provide the multilevel substrate to facilitate the growth rate and survival of coral fragment.

attempts.answer:
Summary and definition of “effectiveness”
Across coral transplantation, “effective” artificial substrates are those that maximize survival and growth of transplanted fragments or settlers, accelerate time-to-coverage, support compatible community assembly, and remain structurally and chemically stable under site conditions over intended deployment durations. Effectiveness is context-dependent: species-specific larval settlement cues and preferences, local hydrodynamics and sedimentation, cost, scalability, and husbandry logistics all shape performance and suitability. Below, we synthesize evidence on which materials perform best and why, highlighting trade-offs that guide selection.

Materials that are broadly effective for transplanting stony corals

1) Modified coral rubble assembled with geotextile nets (low-cost, locally sourced)
- Concept and performance: Wrapping available rubble in inexpensive nylon or polyethylene nets creates a mechanically stable, structurally complex substrate that supports Acropora fragment growth and reduces material costs while using on-site materials. Field pilots reported growth of transplanted corals and replacement of cement-based media, with the main needs being additional multi-site and longer-term testing to confirm replicability. <cite id="1e731c1b-0">Modified coral rubble wrapped with cheap locally available nets formed stable, complex substrates that supported coral growth and replaced concrete/cement-based media in pilot trials; the approach is low-cost and site-available but requires further testing for replicability</cite>.
- Key trade-offs: very low upfront cost and availability; high potential for net degradation and disintegration if not rated to local currents; variability with site conditions; possible vectoring of disease and macroalgal epiphytes if nets are not antifouling treated. <cite id="1e731c1b-0">This rubble-net approach is cheap and locally available but requires testing at additional sites and for longer periods to determine replicability</cite>.

2) Concrete-based modular artificial patch reefs (APRs) and terracotta/earthenware ceramics
- Concept and performance: APRs built from concrete blocks provide multi-level, modular substrates for outplanting Acropora fragments; stabilization with cable ties is widely used and as effective as epoxy or cement. In shallow, turbid waters, multilevel structures can facilitate growth by positioning fragments in preferred hydrodynamic strata; however, lower levels often accumulate sediment, reducing effective substrate area. <cite id="1e731c1b-1">Artificial Patch Reefs made of concrete blocks deployed as multilevel structures facilitated transplanting Acropora; cable ties were widely effective for fixation, similar to epoxy/cement methods</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-2">Multilevel APR substrates may provide hard substrate to facilitate fragment growth in shallow turbid water, but information on survival and growth with multilevel structure is limited</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-1">The base level often covered by resuspended sediment; top-level use avoided to prevent physical damage</cite>.
- Key trade-offs: deployable at scale; durable in structure but susceptible to biofouling and burial at lower levels; alkalinity/leaching risks from uncarbonated or poorly carbonated concrete; cost and transport footprint for large blocks. <cite id="1e731c1b-1">Cement/epoxy-based attachment methods are common and effective; however, concrete structures can be affected by sediment resuspension at lower levels</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-3">Artificial substrates can alter ecological interactions, change structural complexity, and present long-term stability and durability issues compared to natural reefs</cite>.

3) Engineered inorganic settlement substrates tuned for larval cues (lime mortar, quartz, strontianite, bioactive glass; avoid generic earthenware)
- Concept and performance: Choice assays show that larvae detect and respond to mineral cues and microtopography. In two Caribbean taxa (A. palmata, D. labyrinthiformis), quartz sand additives and lime-mortar substrates increased settlement, with strong preference for strontianite in D. labyrinthiformis; generic earthenware ceramic “frag plugs” had some of the lowest settlement rates. These preferences persisted independent of broad roughness/wettability and point to localized topographic features and soluble inorganic minerals (SiO2, SrCO3) guiding attachment. <cite id="8df4b4ee-0">A. palmata larvae slightly preferred quartz sand over bioactive glass, dolomite, strontianite, and earthenware, and D. labyrinthiformis strongly preferred quartz sand or strontianite; earthenware ceramics had some of the lowest settlement</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-4">Larvae exhibited additive-specific preferences independent of mean roughness and wettability, detecting localized topography below body scale and positively responding to soluble inorganic minerals like silica and strontianite</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-3">Quartz sand, borosilicate fibers, and bioactive glass additives were combined in lime mortar; carbonation conversion to CaCO3 exceeded 98% for all additives, with localized aragonite/calcite polymorph shifts</cite>.
- Calcium phosphate (CaP) and lime mortar as biofunctional bases: Lime-mortar-based substrates, when carbonated, provide CaCO3 surfaces with tailored additives; CaP-based composites, leveraging bone-like mineralogy and additive manufacturing, can strongly attract larvae of D. labyrinthiformis, indicating that Ca-based carbonate chemistries and specific ions may enhance settlement and early mineralization. <cite id="8df4b4ee-1">D. labyrinthiformis larvae only settled on substrates made with lime mortar as base material (regardless of additive/topography), and carbonation to CaCO3 >99% was confirmed by PXRD when accelerated in high CO2</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-2">Composite substrates built on lime mortar, CaP (bone-like), acrylic, and PDMS enabled testing of mineral cues; Ca-based systems were selected for further optimization</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-4">Additives including sands, glasses, and alkaline earth carbonates were combined in CaCO3 substrates to increase settlement; minerals such as silica and strontianite were positively sensed</cite>.
- Key trade-offs: lime mortar requires controlled carbonation to avoid high pH from unreacted Ca(OH)2; bioactive glasses can release Ca2+/PO43– and aid initial mineralization but need to be insoluble enough for structural longevity; generic earthenware is often a poor settlement substrate for many taxa. <cite id="8df4b4ee-1">Incomplete carbonation leaves unreacted Ca(OH)2 and high pH that could harm corals, motivating high CO2-accelerated carbonation to >99% conversion to CaCO3</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-3">Bioactive glass is partially soluble, releasing Ca2+ and PO43– ions that can aid CaCO3 mineralization; additives did not strongly inhibit carbonation (>98% conversion), though they altered polymorph composition</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-0">Earthenware ceramic substrates commonly used as frag plugs had some of the lowest settlement rates for both A. palmata and D. labyrinthiformis</cite>.

4) Engineered polymer and 3D-printed scaffolds (biocompatible support, rapid colonization, delivery functions)
- Concept and performance: Porous 3D-printed supports (PLA, polystyrene foams) and soft elastomeric devices can provide high-surface, hydrophobic, low-turbulence microsites that promote rapid fragment attachment and growth; biocompatible films/scaffolds can also serve as wound-healing dressings and drug-delivery platforms for corals. In restoration contexts, 3D-printed “artificial coral skeletons” accelerated growth of attached fragments and supported tissue regeneration, demonstrating that biomaterials can measurably speed transplantation outcomes. <cite id="8c5963e6-0">3D-printed artificial coral skeletons based on polylactic acid ensured fast growth of coral fragments attached to their surface, accelerating transplantation to the reef</cite> <cite id="8c5963e6-0">Biocompatible films (zein–polyvinylpyrrolidone) and ε-caprolactone-p-coumaric acid copolymer supported new coral tissue growth and drug delivery in wounds, highlighting biocompatibility of these polymers toward corals</cite>.
- Bioactive/biodegradable options: Bioinspired CaP and biopolymer scaffolds can be seeded with bioactive glass or growth factors to promote attachment and calcification; their porous coral-like architectures enhance adhesion and vascularization for recolonization. <cite id="8c5963e6-3">Scaffolds may contain bioactive substances (growth factors, ECM) and be coated to guide cell differentiation and tissue regeneration; biomimetic coral bone scaffolds use porous structures akin to natural coral to promote adhesion, proliferation, and vascularization</cite>.
- Key trade-offs: polymers may degrade or leach additives; antifouling and mechanical durability under currents are major concerns; fabrication cost and scalability can be higher than concrete or rubble; regulatory acceptance and long-term ecological effects of biodegradable polymers vary by taxa and site. <cite id="8c5963e6-0">Biodegradable biocomposite films can deliver therapeutics and support tissue growth, but material selection and degradation must be matched to local conditions</cite>.

How material chemistry and surface features shape outcomes

- Mineralogical and ionic cues: Larvae can discriminate CaCO3 polymorphs, silica, strontianite, and bioactive glass additives; quartz-rich sands and strontianite significantly boost settlement for D. labyrinthiformis, whereas generic earthenware ceramics are often suboptimal, indicating that substrate mineralogy and ion release can outweight bulk roughness and wettability in guiding recruitment. <cite id="8df4b4ee-0">Quartz sand outperformed bioactive glass and ceramics for A. palmata; D. labyrinthiformis strongly preferred quartz sand and strontianite; earthenware had lowest settlement</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-4">Larval preferences were additive-specific and independent of mean roughness and wettability, with responses to localized topography and soluble inorganic minerals like SiO2 and SrCO3</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-3">Additives altered polymorph composition (e.g., aragonite detected in quartz- and glass-bearing mortars), highlighting mineral cue specificity</cite>.
- Surface chemistry and topography: Hydrophobic, microstructured polymer surfaces (acrylic, PDMS) and porous inorganic composites can enhance initial attachment, while alkalinity/leachate from uncarbonated cement and pathogen/competitor vectors on inert ceramics can hinder performance. <cite id="8df4b4ee-2">Hydrophobic smooth acrylic surfaces and PDMS were selected to test larval responses; anecdotal evidence suggested hydrophobicity and smoothness might promote attachment and/or discourage algae</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-1">Unreacted Ca(OH)2 from plain lime-mortar substrates can elevate pH, potentially harmful to corals, necessitating full carbonation</cite>.
- Early mineralization: Bioactive glass and CaP additives can supply Ca2+/PO43– ions that aid initial coral polyp calcification, potentially improving survival and growth if the base matrix remains structurally stable. <cite id="8df4b4ee-3">Bioactive glass releases Ca2+ and PO43– ions and aids CaCO3 mineralization; most additives did not strongly inhibit carbonation</cite>.

Selection trade-offs and decision guidance

- Chemical inertness vs. biological activity: High-surface inert concrete, terracotta, or polymer foams are mechanically robust but often lack larval-attractant cues; conversely, bioactive CaP/bioactive glass and lime-mortar composites embed mineralogically informative cues that attract larvae but must be designed for controlled ion release and structural longevity. Choose cue-matched substrates for target taxa and larval supply regimes; where local plankton flux is high, inert substrates may suffice, while low-natural recruitment sites benefit from bioactive cues. <cite id="8df4b4ee-0">Species-specific settlement patterns favor quartz/strontianite cues over generic earthenware</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-4">Larvae detect localized topography and mineral cues, with silica and strontianite being positively responded to</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-1">Carbonated CaCO3 lime-mortar substrates can serve as larval settlement media, but unreacted Ca(OH)2 raises alkalinity risks</cite>.
- Surface roughness and rugosity: While not the sole driver, engineered microtopography and porous scaffolds enhance initial adhesion and polyp orientation; multilevel APRs leverage vertical rugosity for placement within preferred hydrodynamic microenvironments. <cite id="8df4b4ee-4">Localized topographic features more than an order of magnitude below body width can drive settlement choices</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-2">Multilevel APR substrates provide vertical habitat layers to facilitate fragment growth in shallow turbid waters</cite>.
- Mechanical durability, fouling, and burial: Concrete structures are durable but prone to biofouling and sediment burial at lower levels; polymer/foam scaffolds offer colonization surfaces but degrade under UV/currents; rubble-net structures can disintegrate without proper net design and may vector epiphytes; 3D-printed CaP scaffolds need to balance degradation rates with coral growth. <cite id="1e731c1b-1">Lower levels often covered by resuspended sediment, reducing effective substrate</cite> <cite id="8c5963e6-0">3D-printed PLA skeletons accelerated fragment growth, but material degradation and environmental exposure must be managed</cite>.
- Cost, scalability, and husbandry: Net-wrapped rubble is the lowest-cost, most scalable option where locally abundant rubble exists; APRs and terracotta tiles are deployable at scale but heavier and more alkaline-prone; engineered composites and 3D-printed scaffolds offer precise geometry and functions but can be more expensive and require fabrication infrastructure. <cite id="1e731c1b-0">Rubble+net approach is cheap and locally available, replacing cement-based media in growth trials</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-1">Concrete APRs are widely deployable; cable ties are as effective as epoxy/cement for fixation</cite> <cite id="8c5963e6-0">3D-printed artificial skeletons supported faster growth and could be integrated into restoration workflows</cite>.
- Ecological fit and long-term sustainability: Artificial substrates may alter ecological interactions, change structural complexity, and face durability issues; they may not fully replicate natural conditions for all species. Selection should be paired with monitoring of community assembly, pathogen prevalence, and growth after sediment/competitor loads are managed. <cite id="1e731c1b-3">Artificial substrates can present ecological mismatches, altered complexity, and durability concerns; continued monitoring is essential</cite>.

Practical recommendations by scenario

- Low-cost, rapid deployment in rubble fields or storm-affected reefs: Use net-wrapped modified coral rubble to create stable, complex surfaces; supplement with locally available quartz-rich aggregates or strontianite-infused lime mortar “starter tiles” to enhance early larval settlement, and deploy fragments across levels to avoid sediment burial. <cite id="1e731c1b-0">Net-wrapped modified coral rubble replaced concrete media and supported growth in pilot trials</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-1">APR multilevel structures and cable-tie fixation provide a scalable framework</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-0">Quartz sand and strontianite enhance settlement for key Caribbean taxa</cite>.
- Shallow coastal nurseries and outplanting with Acropora: Use concrete APRs or terracotta tiles for durability and ease of fixation; if settling is slow, add lime-mortar-CaP or bioactive glass tiles with controlled carbonation and Ca2+/PO43– additives to attract larvae; design vertical spacing to keep substrates above sediment layers. <cite id="1e731c1b-2">APRs provide multilevel hard substrates to facilitate growth in shallow turbid waters</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-1">Lime mortar carbonated to CaCO3 functions as an effective larval substrate for D. labyrinthiformis</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-3">Bioactive glass additives supply ions aiding CaCO3 mineralization without strongly inhibiting carbonation</cite>.
- Sites with low natural larval supply or target taxa with specific mineralogical cues: Favor engineered CaP/bioactive glass composites and quartz/strontianite-functionalized lime-mortar substrates; minimize use of generic earthenware “frag plugs,” which showed consistently low settlement in comparative assays. <cite id="8df4b4ee-0">Earthenware had some of the lowest settlement rates; quartz/strontianite cues elevated settlement</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-4">Silica and strontianite-specific responses indicate cue-guided selection can increase recruitment</cite>.
- High-tech nurseries or innovative outplanting: Deploy 3D-printed porous PLA or CaP scaffolds to accelerate fragment growth and as drug-delivery supports for tissue repair; integrate biopolymer films for localized antifouling or wound-healing; ensure materials degrade synchronously with coral colonization and are compatible with local currents. <cite id="8c5963e6-0">3D-printed PLA skeletons sped fragment growth; biocompatible films supported drug delivery and tissue regrowth</cite> <cite id="8c5963e6-3">Bioactive/biodegradable scaffolds with growth-factor coatings guide tissue regeneration</cite>.
- Risk management and monitoring: Regardless of material, pre-deploy test panels to measure settlement, calcification, and fouling; manage sedimentation (orientation, hydrodynamics); test for pH spikes from uncarbonated cement and leachates from polymers/bioactives; and evaluate pathogen and competitor settlement trends. <cite id="8df4b4ee-1">High pH from unreacted Ca(OH)2 can harm corals, requiring carbonation verification</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-3">Artificial substrates can alter ecological interactions and structural complexity, necessitating long-term monitoring</cite>.

Key uncertainties and how to resolve them
Evidence is strongest that material mineralogy and microtopography drive larval settlement beyond gross roughness, with generic earthenware often inferior and lime-mortar/CaP/bioactive glass composites performing well when properly carbonated; however, head-to-head, multi-year comparisons of concrete, terracotta, granite, and polymer foams under varying hydrodynamics remain limited. Resolving this requires paired field trials with standardized fragment sizes and taxa across materials, measuring survival, extension, calcification, and community shift over 1–3 years, with parallel lab settlement assays to link mineral cues to performance across species. <cite id="8df4b4ee-4">Larval choices reflect localized topography and mineral cues rather than bulk wettability/roughness</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-0">Earthenware’s low settlement and quartz/strontianite preferences demonstrate cue specificity</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-1">Concrete APRs and fixation methods are effective but sedimentation constrains lower levels</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-0">Rubble+net substrates are effective and low-cost but need broader replication</cite>.

Bottom line
- Best-performing classes in practice:
  - Modified coral rubble assembled with durable nets when local rubble is abundant and hydrodynamics allow, for rapid, low-cost deployment and growth. <cite id="1e731c1b-0">Net-wrapped modified coral rubble supported Acropora growth and replaced cement media</cite>.
  - Concrete APRs and terracotta tiles for large-scale, modular outplanting; enhance with lime-mortar-CaP/bioactive glass “starter tiles” where recruitment is slow, and position panels to avoid burial. <cite id="1e731c1b-1">APRs with cable-tie fixation are deployable and effective</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-1">Carbonated lime mortar strongly supports D. labyrinthiformis settlement</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-3">Bioactive glass additives can aid early mineralization</cite>.
  - Engineered polymers and 3D-printed CaP/PLA scaffolds to accelerate growth and enable delivery/antifouling functions, particularly in nurseries and targeted outplants. <cite id="8c5963e6-0">3D-printed artificial coral skeletons accelerated growth and supported biocompatible delivery systems</cite>.
- Worst-performing general-purpose ceramic: Generic earthenware/terracotta “frag plugs” for many taxa due to low settlement; prefer cue-engineered alternatives. <cite id="8df4b4ee-0">Earthenware ceramics had some of the lowest settlement rates across species</cite>.
- Trade-offs dominate selection: cue-matched bioactivity vs. long-term structural integrity; hydrodynamic placement vs. sedimentation; cost/scalability vs. performance; chemical stability vs. initial attraction. Choose materials and configurations validated for your taxa and hydrodynamics, and manage for fouling and alkalinity/leaching risk. <cite id="8df4b4ee-4">Larval responses hinge on localized topography and mineral cues</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-1">Carbonation status of lime mortar affects pH safety</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-3">Artificial substrates entail ecological fit and durability trade-offs requiring monitoring</cite>.

Title: Coral transplantation on a multilevel substrate of Artificial Patch Reefs: effect of fixing methods on the growth rate of two Acropora species
Snippet: Coral fragments were collected from donor site of two Acropora species in the inner lagoon and in front of the reef flat of Panjang Island. Fragments of A. aspera were collected by broken off small branches at random mother colonies while A. copiosa fragments were chisel off main branches of adult colonies randomly. The small branches of two species (average size was 12.57 cm 3 ) were transferred into basket and then were transplanted on multilevel substrates of Artificial Patch Reefs (APR) which deployed in the eastern site of Panjang Island. Artificial Patch Reefs (APR) is artificial reefs made by concrete blocks composed as modular circular structures in shape, constructed 5 (five) levels of substrates were deployed from small boats by SCUBA divers, and are suitable near natural reefs in shallow water. The total height of the multilevel APR structure is about 120 cm from the bottom of the sea, and the height of each level is 20 cm. In this experiment, coral fragments were transplanted in the upper, middle, and lower level. Coral transplantation experiments were not applied at the top level to prevent physical damage in coral fragments. The experiments were also not implemented in the coral transplantation in the base of APR (level 5) since the surface of the substrate usually covering sediment due to resuspension (Figure 2). At the beginning of November 2018, 120 coral fragments were transplanted on three levels of APR by two fixation methods: vertically and horizontally orientation of the fragments fixing on the surface of substrates and tied to a paired of the nail using cable ties (Figure 3). Cable ties method of coral transplantation has been widely applied and effective technique for attaching Acropora fragments to artificial substrate (William and Miller 2010;Young et al. 2012). Coral fragment stabilization using cable ties was similarly effective to epoxy or cement methods (William and Miller 2010).
</snippet>

Title: Coral transplantation on a multilevel substrate of Artificial Patch Reefs: effect of fixing methods on the growth rate of two Acropora species
Snippet: In order to optimize reef rehabilitation, combining artificial reefs and coral transplantation is recommended (Abelson 2006;Ammar et al. 2013;Cummings et al. 2015). 

Artificial Patch Reefs (APR) is an artificial structure which is applied to rehabilitate coral reef in order to develop shallow water habitat (Munasik et al. 2018). APR is a rehabilitation tool that is designed by multilevel substrates and applied the combination both of coral transplantation and artificial reefs. Acropora spp. is generally considered as a good for candidates for use in coral transplantation or population enhancement project due to their high growth rate and high survivorship of fragments (Lirman et al. 2010;Boch and Morse 2012;Mercado-Molina 2016;Schopmeyer et al. 2017). The application of APR with Acropora transplanted on their substrates is considered contributing to the local conservation of the small island reefs in the near future. In this study, two Acropora species were selected and applied to investigate the suitable method and species selection for reef rehabilitation. Multilevel substrates of APR may provide the hard substrate to facilitate fragment of coral grows in shallow turbid water. However, the information about the effect of multilevel substrates on survival and growth of transplanted corals is limited. This study aims to address the effectiveness of the APR structure to provide the multilevel substrate to facilitate the growth rate and survival of coral fragment.
</snippet>

Title: Successful establishment of a coral nursery for active reef restoration in Kavaratti Island, Lakshadweep archipelago
Snippet: The coral transplantation on artificial substrates in the shallow lagoon off the Lakshadweep archipelago has shown promising results in establishing a coral nursery, promoting coral growth and providing a habitat for marine life. The establishment of a coral nursery has led to increased fish aggregation, contributing to enhanced biodiversity and ecosystem resilience. These findings highlight the potential of this restoration technique as a valuable tool in reef conservation efforts for vulnerable ecosystems such as those found in the Lakshadweep archipelago. However, the use of artificial substrates instead of transplanting corals directly onto degraded reefs may present certain limitations, such as differences in the ecological interactions between the artificial and natural environments, potential changes in the structural complexity, and the long-term stability and durability of the artificial substrates. Additionally, the artificial substrates may not fully replicate the conditions necessary for the growth and survival of certain coral species. Continued monitoring and research are essential to assess the long-term effectiveness and sustainability of this approach.
</snippet>

Title: Engineered Substrates Reveal Species-Specific Inorganic Cues for Coral Larval Settlement
Snippet: At the outset of this project, we tested a range of materials that could serve as a base material for fabricating coral settlement substrates, which could be subsequently modified to investigate larval preferences. The candidates for base material were selected based on their availability and cost, ease of fabrication and/or modification, and for a diversity of compositions. The first material selected for testing was lime mortar, a calcite (CaCO3)-based material produced from hydrated lime (also known as kalkwasser powder by aquarists) that is used in the restoration of historic buildings. 52 Notably, coral skeletons are also made of CaCO3, although in its aragonite form. The second material selected was calcium phosphate (CaP), the primary mineral component of vertebrate bone. Our group has expertise in additive manufacturing of CaP scaffolds for bone regeneration, [53][54] and this represented an opportunity to transfer knowledge from tissue engineering to coral reef restoration. In addition to these Ca-based mineral systems, two engineered polymers were also selected. The first was poly(methyl methacrylate), or acrylic, which is used widely in the aquarium hobby. Anecdotal observations also suggested that the hydrophobicity and smoothness of this material might promote attachment by the hydrophobic coral larvae and/or discourage algal attachment. The final base material selected was polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), a transparent moldable elastomer often utilized in microfluidics and microfabrication. 55 The use of PDMS in antifouling applications also suggested a potential benefit to settling coral larvae if this material promoted coral attachment and/or inhibited algal fouling. 40

Title: Engineered Substrates Reveal Species-Specific Inorganic Cues for Coral Larval Settlement
Snippet: To investigate the settlement preferences of coral larvae in response to diverse inorganic cues, we modified the base lime mortar material with two additives from each of three material groups: (1) natural sands, (2) synthetic glasses, and (3) alkaline earth carbonates (Fig. 3). Natural sands are traditionally used as the "aggregate" that adds strength to mortars and cements. 61 From this category, we selected a standard, quartz-rich sand and a high-aragonite sand. The selection of two different types of sand enabled the comparison of larval preference for an abundant non-Ca-based mineral (here, silica/quartz) and the mineral found in abundance on reefs in both the skeletons of living corals and the reef structure that they leave behind (i.e., aragonite). From glasses, we selected borosilicate glass fibers and a bioactive glass powder. Glass fibers are a standard insoluble material added to increase the strength of composite resins, and bioactive glasses are partially soluble silicates that release Ca 2+ and PO4 3-ions and aid in bone growth 62 and CaCO3 mineralization. 63 Finally, we also selected two alkaline earth carbonate additives: strontianite (SrCO3) and dolomite (CaMg(CO3)2). ] We hypothesized that the presence of these elements in substrates could influence larval settlement and might even aid in the initial mineralization and survival of settled polyps. 

We investigated the effect of these additives on both mortar carbonation and the final structure of the substrates after carbonation was complete. None of the additives strongly inhibited carbonation (>98% conversion for all additives). However, most additives did affect the final polymorphism of the mortar. In addition to calcite, the presence of aragonite was detected in substrates containing quartz sand (1 wt% aragonite), glass fibers (1.5 wt%), bioactive glass (0.9 wt%), strontianite (22.7 wt%), and in substrates containing the combination of dolomite and strontianite (6.4 wt%; Fig. S7).

Snippet: : The widespread loss of stony reef-building coral populations has been compounded by the low settlement and survival of coral juveniles. To rebuild coral communities, restoration practitioners have developed work ﬂ ows to settle vulnerable coral larvae in the laboratory and outplant settled juveniles back to natural and arti ﬁ cial reefs. These work ﬂ ows often make use of natural biochemical settlement cues, which are presented to swimming larvae to induce settlement. This paper establishes the potential for inorganic cues to complement these known biochemical e ﬀ ects. Settlement substrates were fabricated from calcium carbonate, a material present naturally on reefs, and modi ﬁ ed with additives including sands, glasses, and alkaline earth carbonates. Experiments with larvae of two Caribbean coral species revealed additive-speci ﬁ c settlement preferences that were independent of bulk surface properties such as mean roughness and wettability. Instead, analyses of the substrates suggest that settling coral larvae can detect localized topographical features more than an order of magnitude smaller than their body width and can sense and positively respond to soluble inorganic minerals such as silica (SiO 2 ) and strontianite (SrCO 3 ). These ﬁ ndings open a new area of research in coral reef restoration, in which composite substrates can be designed with a combination of natural organic and inorganic additives to increase larval settlement and perhaps also improve post-settlement growth, mineralization, and defense. of the lime mortar fabrication process and the fabrication of additional substrate types are provided in the Supporting Information along with details on substrate characterization methods. Title: Mechanistic study on the role of 3D-Printed biomimetic coral bone scaffolds in bone defect repair
Snippet: The preparation process and material characteristics of 3D-printed biomimetic coral bone scaffolds are crucial factors for the successful application of this technology in bone defect repair. The successful preparation of 3D-printed biomimetic coral bone scaffolds begins with the selection of materials. Commonly used materials include biodegradable polymers, bioceramics, and bioactive substances. These materials need to exhibit excellent biocompatibility, compatibility with human tissues, and gradual degradation over a specific period. The preparation process starts with Computer-Aided Design (CAD), where a digital model defines the scaffold's geometric shape and internal structure. This step forms the basis for personalized fabrication, allowing customized design based on the specific bone defect conditions of patients to enhance repair effectiveness [8]. Utilizing layer-by-layer manufacturing technology, the digital model is segmented into layers and printed layer by layer. 3D printing technology precisely overlays materials according to the predefined CAD model, achieving accurate threedimensional structural preparation. This step determines the final form and internal structure of the scaffold. After preparation, the scaffold may undergo post-processing steps, such as removing residual scaffold materials and surface polishing, ensuring a smooth, non-toxic surface with appropriate mechanical properties. The uniqueness of biomimetic coral bone scaffolds lies in their porous structure, simulating the microstructure of natural coral bones. This porous structure provides an ideal environment for cell growth, aiding in the attachment, growth, and differentiation of bone cells. The biocompatibility of the printing material is crucial to ensure that the scaffold does not induce noticeable immune reactions or rejection when implanted in the body. The selection of biodegradable materials promotes gradual scaffold degradation and integration with surrounding tissues. Materials must possess sufficient biomechanical properties to withstand bone loads and provide necessary mechanical support. Biomaterials like bioceramics often exhibit good biomechanical properties, adapting to the mechanical requirements of bone tissue. Some scaffolds may contain bioactive substances, such as growth factors or drugs, to promote cell proliferation, differentiation, or inhibit inflammatory reactions, thereby accelerating the healing process of bone defects [9].
</snippet>

The scaffold surface can be coated with bioactive substances such as growth factors and extracellular matrix components. Scaffold design not only considers microstructure but also focuses on its biomechanical properties [10]. This personalized customization capability enhances the precision of treatment, enabling the scaffold to better adapt to the specific needs of the patient [10]. Overall, 3D-printed biomimetic coral bone scaffolds, through meticulous preparation processes and excellent material characteristics, provide a viable solution for personalized and efficient bone defect repair. These features enable the scaffold to better adapt to the physiological and anatomical structures of patients, thereby improving the success rate of treatment.

Summary and definition of “effectiveness”
Across coral transplantation, “effective” artificial substrates are those that maximize survival and growth of transplanted fragments or settlers, accelerate time-to-coverage, support compatible community assembly, and remain structurally and chemically stable under site conditions over intended deployment durations. Effectiveness is context-dependent: species-specific larval settlement cues and preferences, local hydrodynamics and sedimentation, cost, scalability, and husbandry logistics all shape performance and suitability. Below, we synthesize evidence on which materials perform best and why, highlighting trade-offs that guide selection.

Materials that are broadly effective for transplanting stony corals

1) Modified coral rubble assembled with geotextile nets (low-cost, locally sourced)
- Concept and performance: Wrapping available rubble in inexpensive nylon or polyethylene nets creates a mechanically stable, structurally complex substrate that supports Acropora fragment growth and reduces material costs while using on-site materials. Field pilots reported growth of transplanted corals and replacement of cement-based media, with the main needs being additional multi-site and longer-term testing to confirm replicability. <cite id="1e731c1b-0">Modified coral rubble wrapped with cheap locally available nets formed stable, complex substrates that supported coral growth and replaced concrete/cement-based media in pilot trials; the approach is low-cost and site-available but requires further testing for replicability</cite>.
- Key trade-offs: very low upfront cost and availability; high potential for net degradation and disintegration if not rated to local currents; variability with site conditions; possible vectoring of disease and macroalgal epiphytes if nets are not antifouling treated. <cite id="1e731c1b-0">This rubble-net approach is cheap and locally available but requires testing at additional sites and for longer periods to determine replicability</cite>.

2) Concrete-based modular artificial patch reefs (APRs) and terracotta/earthenware ceramics
- Concept and performance: APRs built from concrete blocks provide multi-level, modular substrates for outplanting Acropora fragments; stabilization with cable ties is widely used and as effective as epoxy or cement. In shallow, turbid waters, multilevel structures can facilitate growth by positioning fragments in preferred hydrodynamic strata; however, lower levels often accumulate sediment, reducing effective substrate area. <cite id="1e731c1b-1">Artificial Patch Reefs made of concrete blocks deployed as multilevel structures facilitated transplanting Acropora; cable ties were widely effective for fixation, similar to epoxy/cement methods</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-2">Multilevel APR substrates may provide hard substrate to facilitate fragment growth in shallow turbid water, but information on survival and growth with multilevel structure is limited</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-1">The base level often covered by resuspended sediment; top-level use avoided to prevent physical damage</cite>.
- Key trade-offs: deployable at scale; durable in structure but susceptible to biofouling and burial at lower levels; alkalinity/leaching risks from uncarbonated or poorly carbonated concrete; cost and transport footprint for large blocks. <cite id="1e731c1b-1">Cement/epoxy-based attachment methods are common and effective; however, concrete structures can be affected by sediment resuspension at lower levels</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-3">Artificial substrates can alter ecological interactions, change structural complexity, and present long-term stability and durability issues compared to natural reefs</cite>.

In two Caribbean taxa (A. palmata, D. labyrinthiformis), quartz sand additives and lime-mortar substrates increased settlement, with strong preference for strontianite in D. labyrinthiformis; generic earthenware ceramic “frag plugs” had some of the lowest settlement rates. These preferences persisted independent of broad roughness/wettability and point to localized topographic features and soluble inorganic minerals (SiO2, SrCO3) guiding attachment. <cite id="8df4b4ee-0">A. palmata larvae slightly preferred quartz sand over bioactive glass, dolomite, strontianite, and earthenware, and D. labyrinthiformis strongly preferred quartz sand or strontianite; earthenware ceramics had some of the lowest settlement</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-4">Larvae exhibited additive-specific preferences independent of mean roughness and wettability, detecting localized topography below body scale and positively responding to soluble inorganic minerals like silica and strontianite</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-3">Quartz sand, borosilicate fibers, and bioactive glass additives were combined in lime mortar; carbonation conversion to CaCO3 exceeded 98% for all additives, with localized aragonite/calcite polymorph shifts</cite>.
- Calcium phosphate (CaP) and lime mortar as biofunctional bases: Lime-mortar-based substrates, when carbonated, provide CaCO3 surfaces with tailored additives; CaP-based composites, leveraging bone-like mineralogy and additive manufacturing, can strongly attract larvae of D. labyrinthiformis, indicating that Ca-based carbonate chemistries and specific ions may enhance settlement and early mineralization. <cite id="8df4b4ee-1">D. labyrinthiformis larvae only settled on substrates made with lime mortar as base material (regardless of additive/topography), and carbonation to CaCO3 >99% was confirmed by PXRD when accelerated in high CO2</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-2">Composite substrates built on lime mortar, CaP (bone-like), acrylic, and PDMS enabled testing of mineral cues; Ca-based systems were selected for further optimization</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-4">Additives including sands, glasses, and alkaline earth carbonates were combined in CaCO3 substrates to increase settlement; minerals such as silica and strontianite were positively sensed</cite>.
- Key trade-offs: lime mortar requires controlled carbonation to avoid high pH from unreacted Ca(OH)2; bioactive glasses can release Ca2+/PO43– and aid initial mineralization but need to be insoluble enough for structural longevity; generic earthenware is often a poor settlement substrate for many taxa. <cite id="8df4b4ee-1">Incomplete carbonation leaves unreacted Ca(OH)2 and high pH that could harm corals, motivating high CO2-accelerated carbonation to >99% conversion to CaCO3</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-3">Bioactive glass is partially soluble, releasing Ca2+ and PO43– ions that can aid CaCO3 mineralization; additives did not strongly inhibit carbonation (>98% conversion), though they altered polymorph composition</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-0">Earthenware ceramic substrates commonly used as frag plugs had some of the lowest settlement rates for both A. palmata and D. labyrinthiformis</cite>.

4) Engineered polymer and 3D-printed scaffolds (biocompatible support, rapid colonization, delivery functions)
- Concept and performance: Porous 3D-printed supports (PLA, polystyrene foams) and soft elastomeric devices can provide high-surface, hydrophobic, low-turbulence microsites that promote rapid fragment attachment and growth; biocompatible films/scaffolds can also serve as wound-healing dressings and drug-delivery platforms for corals. In restoration contexts, 3D-printed “artificial coral skeletons” accelerated growth of attached fragments and supported tissue regeneration, demonstrating that biomaterials can measurably speed transplantation outcomes. <cite id="8c5963e6-0">3D-printed artificial coral skeletons based on polylactic acid ensured fast growth of coral fragments attached to their surface, accelerating transplantation to the reef</cite> <cite id="8c5963e6-0">Biocompatible films (zein–polyvinylpyrrolidone) and ε-caprolactone-p-coumaric acid copolymer supported new coral tissue growth and drug delivery in wounds, highlighting biocompatibility of these polymers toward corals</cite>.
- Bioactive/biodegradable options: Bioinspired CaP and biopolymer scaffolds can be seeded with bioactive glass or growth factors to promote attachment and calcification; their porous coral-like architectures enhance adhesion and vascularization for recolonization. <cite id="8c5963e6-3">Scaffolds may contain bioactive substances (growth factors, ECM) and be coated to guide cell differentiation and tissue regeneration; biomimetic coral bone scaffolds use porous structures akin to natural coral to promote adhesion, proliferation, and vascularization</cite>.
- Key trade-offs: polymers may degrade or leach additives; antifouling and mechanical durability under currents are major concerns; fabrication cost and scalability can be higher than concrete or rubble; regulatory acceptance and long-term ecological effects of biodegradable polymers vary by taxa and site. <cite id="8c5963e6-0">Biodegradable biocomposite films can deliver therapeutics and support tissue growth, but material selection and degradation must be matched to local conditions</cite>.

How material chemistry and surface features shape outcomes

- Mineralogical and ionic cues: Larvae can discriminate CaCO3 polymorphs, silica, strontianite, and bioactive glass additives; quartz-rich sands and strontianite significantly boost settlement for D. labyrinthiformis, whereas generic earthenware ceramics are often suboptimal, indicating that substrate mineralogy and ion release can outweight bulk roughness and wettability in guiding recruitment. <cite id="8df4b4ee-0">Quartz sand outperformed bioactive glass and ceramics for A. palmata; D. labyrinthiformis strongly preferred quartz sand and strontianite; earthenware had lowest settlement</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-4">Larval preferences were additive-specific and independent of mean roughness and wettability, with responses to localized topography and soluble inorganic minerals like SiO2 and SrCO3</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-3">Additives altered polymorph composition (e.g., aragonite detected in quartz- and glass-bearing mortars), highlighting mineral cue specificity</cite>.
- Surface chemistry and topography: Hydrophobic, microstructured polymer surfaces (acrylic, PDMS) and porous inorganic composites can enhance initial attachment, while alkalinity/leachate from uncarbonated cement and pathogen/competitor vectors on inert ceramics can hinder performance. <cite id="8df4b4ee-2">Hydrophobic smooth acrylic surfaces and PDMS were selected to test larval responses; anecdotal evidence suggested hydrophobicity and smoothness might promote attachment and/or discourage algae</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-1">Unreacted Ca(OH)2 from plain lime-mortar substrates can elevate pH, potentially harmful to corals, necessitating full carbonation</cite>.
- Early mineralization: Bioactive glass and CaP additives can supply Ca2+/PO43– ions that aid initial coral polyp calcification, potentially improving survival and growth if the base matrix remains structurally stable. <cite id="8df4b4ee-3">Bioactive glass releases Ca2+ and PO43– ions and aids CaCO3 mineralization; most additives did not strongly inhibit carbonation</cite>.

Selection trade-offs and decision guidance

- Chemical inertness vs. biological activity: High-surface inert concrete, terracotta, or polymer foams are mechanically robust but often lack larval-attractant cues; conversely, bioactive CaP/bioactive glass and lime-mortar composites embed mineralogically informative cues that attract larvae but must be designed for controlled ion release and structural longevity. Choose cue-matched substrates for target taxa and larval supply regimes; where local plankton flux is high, inert substrates may suffice, while low-natural recruitment sites benefit from bioactive cues. <cite id="8df4b4ee-0">Species-specific settlement patterns favor quartz/strontianite cues over generic earthenware</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-4">Larvae detect localized topography and mineral cues, with silica and strontianite being positively responded to</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-1">Carbonated CaCO3 lime-mortar substrates can serve as larval settlement media, but unreacted Ca(OH)2 raises alkalinity risks</cite>.
- Surface roughness and rugosity: While not the sole driver, engineered microtopography and porous scaffolds enhance initial adhesion and polyp orientation; multilevel APRs leverage vertical rugosity for placement within preferred hydrodynamic microenvironments. <cite id="8df4b4ee-4">Localized topographic features more than an order of magnitude below body width can drive settlement choices</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-2">Multilevel APR substrates provide vertical habitat layers to facilitate fragment growth in shallow turbid waters</cite>.
- Mechanical durability, fouling, and burial: Concrete structures are durable but prone to biofouling and sediment burial at lower levels; polymer/foam scaffolds offer colonization surfaces but degrade under UV/currents; rubble-net structures can disintegrate without proper net design and may vector epiphytes; 3D-printed CaP scaffolds need to balance degradation rates with coral growth. <cite id="1e731c1b-1">Lower levels often covered by resuspended sediment, reducing effective substrate</cite> <cite id="8c5963e6-0">3D-printed PLA skeletons accelerated fragment growth, but material degradation and environmental exposure must be managed</cite>.
- Cost, scalability, and husbandry: Net-wrapped rubble is the lowest-cost, most scalable option where locally abundant rubble exists; APRs and terracotta tiles are deployable at scale but heavier and more alkaline-prone; engineered composites and 3D-printed scaffolds offer precise geometry and functions but can be more expensive and require fabrication infrastructure. <cite id="1e731c1b-0">Rubble+net approach is cheap and locally available, replacing cement-based media in growth trials</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-1">Concrete APRs are widely deployable; cable ties are as effective as epoxy/cement for fixation</cite> <cite id="8c5963e6-0">3D-printed artificial skeletons supported faster growth and could be integrated into restoration workflows</cite>.
- Ecological fit and long-term sustainability: Artificial substrates may alter ecological interactions, change structural complexity, and face durability issues; they may not fully replicate natural conditions for all species. Selection should be paired with monitoring of community assembly, pathogen prevalence, and growth after sediment/competitor loads are managed. <cite id="1e731c1b-3">Artificial substrates can present ecological mismatches, altered complexity, and durability concerns; continued monitoring is essential</cite>.

Practical recommendations by scenario

- Low-cost, rapid deployment in rubble fields or storm-affected reefs: Use net-wrapped modified coral rubble to create stable, complex surfaces; supplement with locally available quartz-rich aggregates or strontianite-infused lime mortar “starter tiles” to enhance early larval settlement, and deploy fragments across levels to avoid sediment burial. <cite id="1e731c1b-0">Net-wrapped modified coral rubble replaced concrete media and supported growth in pilot trials</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-1">APR multilevel structures and cable-tie fixation provide a scalable framework</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-0">Quartz sand and strontianite enhance settlement for key Caribbean taxa</cite>.
- Shallow coastal nurseries and outplanting with Acropora: Use concrete APRs or terracotta tiles for durability and ease of fixation; if settling is slow, add lime-mortar-CaP or bioactive glass tiles with controlled carbonation and Ca2+/PO43– additives to attract larvae; design vertical spacing to keep substrates above sediment layers. <cite id="1e731c1b-2">APRs provide multilevel hard substrates to facilitate growth in shallow turbid waters</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-1">Lime mortar carbonated to CaCO3 functions as an effective larval substrate for D. labyrinthiformis</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-3">Bioactive glass additives supply ions aiding CaCO3 mineralization without strongly inhibiting carbonation</cite>.
- Sites with low natural larval supply or target taxa with specific mineralogical cues: Favor engineered CaP/bioactive glass composites and quartz/strontianite-functionalized lime-mortar substrates; minimize use of generic earthenware “frag plugs,” which showed consistently low settlement in comparative assays. <cite id="8df4b4ee-0">Earthenware had some of the lowest settlement rates; quartz/strontianite cues elevated settlement</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-4">Silica and strontianite-specific responses indicate cue-guided selection can increase recruitment</cite>.
- High-tech nurseries or innovative outplanting: Deploy 3D-printed porous PLA or CaP scaffolds to accelerate fragment growth and as drug-delivery supports for tissue repair; integrate biopolymer films for localized antifouling or wound-healing; ensure materials degrade synchronously with coral colonization and are compatible with local currents. <cite id="8c5963e6-0">3D-printed PLA skeletons sped fragment growth; biocompatible films supported drug delivery and tissue regrowth</cite> <cite id="8c5963e6-3">Bioactive/biodegradable scaffolds with growth-factor coatings guide tissue regeneration</cite>.
- Risk management and monitoring: Regardless of material, pre-deploy test panels to measure settlement, calcification, and fouling; manage sedimentation (orientation, hydrodynamics); test for pH spikes from uncarbonated cement and leachates from polymers/bioactives; and evaluate pathogen and competitor settlement trends. <cite id="8df4b4ee-1">High pH from unreacted Ca(OH)2 can harm corals, requiring carbonation verification</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-3">Artificial substrates can alter ecological interactions and structural complexity, necessitating long-term monitoring</cite>.

Key uncertainties and how to resolve them
Evidence is strongest that material mineralogy and microtopography drive larval settlement beyond gross roughness, with generic earthenware often inferior and lime-mortar/CaP/bioactive glass composites performing well when properly carbonated; however, head-to-head, multi-year comparisons of concrete, terracotta, granite, and polymer foams under varying hydrodynamics remain limited. Resolving this requires paired field trials with standardized fragment sizes and taxa across materials, measuring survival, extension, calcification, and community shift over 1–3 years, with parallel lab settlement assays to link mineral cues to performance across species. <cite id="8df4b4ee-4">Larval choices reflect localized topography and mineral cues rather than bulk wettability/roughness</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-0">Earthenware’s low settlement and quartz/strontianite preferences demonstrate cue specificity</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-1">Concrete APRs and fixation methods are effective but sedimentation constrains lower levels</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-0">Rubble+net substrates are effective and low-cost but need broader replication</cite>.

Bottom line
- Best-performing classes in practice:
  - Modified coral rubble assembled with durable nets when local rubble is abundant and hydrodynamics allow, for rapid, low-cost deployment and growth. <cite id="1e731c1b-0">Net-wrapped modified coral rubble supported Acropora growth and replaced cement media</cite>.
  - Concrete APRs and terracotta tiles for large-scale, modular outplanting; enhance with lime-mortar-CaP/bioactive glass “starter tiles” where recruitment is slow, and position panels to avoid burial. <cite id="1e731c1b-1">APRs with cable-tie fixation are deployable and effective</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-1">Carbonated lime mortar strongly supports D. labyrinthiformis settlement</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-3">Bioactive glass additives can aid early mineralization</cite>.
  - Engineered polymers and 3D-printed CaP/PLA scaffolds to accelerate growth and enable delivery/antifouling functions, particularly in nurseries and targeted outplants. <cite id="8c5963e6-0">3D-printed artificial coral skeletons accelerated growth and supported biocompatible delivery systems</cite>.
- Worst-performing general-purpose ceramic: Generic earthenware/terracotta “frag plugs” for many taxa due to low settlement; prefer cue-engineered alternatives. <cite id="8df4b4ee-0">Earthenware ceramics had some of the lowest settlement rates across species</cite>.
- Trade-offs dominate selection: cue-matched bioactivity vs. long-term structural integrity; hydrodynamic placement vs. sedimentation; cost/scalability vs. performance; chemical stability vs. initial attraction. Choose materials and configurations validated for your taxa and hydrodynamics, and manage for fouling and alkalinity/leaching risk. <cite id="8df4b4ee-4">Larval responses hinge on localized topography and mineral cues</cite> <cite id="8df4b4ee-1">Carbonation status of lime mortar affects pH safety</cite> <cite id="1e731c1b-3">Artificial substrates entail ecological fit and durability trade-offs requiring monitoring</cite>.

Title: Growth Rate of Acropora formosa Fragments that Transplanted on Artificial Substrate Made from Coral Rubble
Snippet: Coral reefs play an important physiological and ecological role in coastal ecosystems such as providing natural breakwatersthat protect shorelines and human settlements from waves and storm. Corals killed by tsunami, waves and storms are often degraded into rubble. This rubble is dynamic, easily shifted by currents and storms, which effectively forms â€˜â€˜killing fieldsâ€™â€™ forcoral juveniles, hindering coral recovery. In order to rehabilitate coral reefs, artificial substrates are used both for coral transplantation and recruitment. Unfortunately, most artificial substrates are expensive and use land-based material such asconcrete/cement-bases. In order to develop a new low-cost artificial substrate that can replace concrete/cement-base as amedia for coral transplantation, modified coral rubble was tested in a pilot study in Seribu Island, Jakarta. Two different nets (nylon and polyethylene) were used to form rubble into a compact shape, stable and strong substrate. The stability of therubble and the complexity of the surface which is created by the net make this substrate suitable for coral transplantation.Additionally, from an economic perspective the nets are very cheap and locally available. In a number of experiments,modified coral rubble successfully replaced the concrete /cement-base as a media for coral transplantation. The coral transplants were growing over time. With this method, we can try to rehabilitate the degraded coral reef destroyed by tsunami or other factors with material that already is available at the site and with less money. However, this approach requires testing at additional sites and for longer periods, to determine the replicability of the results.Key words: cement base, coral, rubble, transplantation

Title: Coral transplantation on a multilevel substrate of Artificial Patch Reefs: effect of fixing methods on the growth rate of two Acropora species
Snippet: Coral fragments were collected from donor site of two Acropora species in the inner lagoon and in front of the reef flat of Panjang Island. Fragments of A. aspera were collected by broken off small branches at random mother colonies while A. copiosa fragments were chisel off main branches of adult colonies randomly. The small branches of two species (average size was 12.57 cm 3 ) were transferred into basket and then were transplanted on multilevel substrates of Artificial Patch Reefs (APR) which deployed in the eastern site of Panjang Island. Artificial Patch Reefs (APR) is artificial reefs made by concrete blocks composed as modular circular structures in shape, constructed 5 (five) levels of substrates were deployed from small boats by SCUBA divers, and are suitable near natural reefs in shallow water. The total height of the multilevel APR structure is about 120 cm from the bottom of the sea, and the height of each level is 20 cm. In this experiment, coral fragments were transplanted in the upper, middle, and lower level. Coral transplantation experiments were not applied at the top level to prevent physical damage in coral fragments. The experiments were also not implemented in the coral transplantation in the base of APR (level 5) since the surface of the substrate usually covering sediment due to resuspension (Figure 2). At the beginning of November 2018, 120 coral fragments were transplanted on three levels of APR by two fixation methods: vertically and horizontally orientation of the fragments fixing on the surface of substrates and tied to a paired of the nail using cable ties (Figure 3). Cable ties method of coral transplantation has been widely applied and effective technique for attaching Acropora fragments to artificial substrate (William and Miller 2010;Young et al. 2012). Coral fragment stabilization using cable ties was similarly effective to epoxy or cement methods (William and Miller 2010).

Title: Coral transplantation on a multilevel substrate of Artificial Patch Reefs: effect of fixing methods on the growth rate of two Acropora species
Snippet: In order to optimize reef rehabilitation, combining artificial reefs and coral transplantation is recommended (Abelson 2006;Ammar et al. 2013;Cummings et al. 2015). 

Artificial Patch Reefs (APR) is an artificial structure which is applied to rehabilitate coral reef in order to develop shallow water habitat (Munasik et al. 2018). APR is a rehabilitation tool that is designed by multilevel substrates and applied the combination both of coral transplantation and artificial reefs. Acropora spp. is generally considered as a good for candidates for use in coral transplantation or population enhancement project due to their high growth rate and high survivorship of fragments (Lirman et al. 2010;Boch and Morse 2012;Mercado-Molina 2016;Schopmeyer et al. 2017). The application of APR with Acropora transplanted on their substrates is considered contributing to the local conservation of the small island reefs in the near future. In this study, two Acropora species were selected and applied to investigate the suitable method and species selection for reef rehabilitation. Multilevel substrates of APR may provide the hard substrate to facilitate fragment of coral grows in shallow turbid water. However, the information about the effect of multilevel substrates on survival and growth of transplanted corals is limited. This study aims to address the effectiveness of the APR structure to provide the multilevel substrate to facilitate the growth rate and survival of coral fragment.

Title: Successful establishment of a coral nursery for active reef restoration in Kavaratti Island, Lakshadweep archipelago
Snippet: The coral transplantation on artificial substrates in the shallow lagoon off the Lakshadweep archipelago has shown promising results in establishing a coral nursery, promoting coral growth and providing a habitat for marine life. The establishment of a coral nursery has led to increased fish aggregation, contributing to enhanced biodiversity and ecosystem resilience. These findings highlight the potential of this restoration technique as a valuable tool in reef conservation efforts for vulnerable ecosystems such as those found in the Lakshadweep archipelago. However, the use of artificial substrates instead of transplanting corals directly onto degraded reefs may present certain limitations, such as differences in the ecological interactions between the artificial and natural environments, potential changes in the structural complexity, and the long-term stability and durability of the artificial substrates. Additionally, the artificial substrates may not fully replicate the conditions necessary for the growth and survival of certain coral species. Continued monitoring and research are essential to assess the long-term effectiveness and sustainability of this approach.

documents.snippet: Coral fragments were collected from donor site of two Acropora species in the inner lagoon and in front of the reef flat of Panjang Island. Fragments of A. aspera were collected by broken off small branches at random mother colonies while A. copiosa fragments were chisel off main branches of adult colonies randomly. The small branches of two species (average size was 12.57 cm 3 ) were transferred into basket and then were transplanted on multilevel substrates of Artificial Patch Reefs (APR) which deployed in the eastern site of Panjang Island. Artificial Patch Reefs (APR) is artificial reefs made by concrete blocks composed as modular circular structures in shape, constructed 5 (five) levels of substrates were deployed from small boats by SCUBA divers, and are suitable near natural reefs in shallow water. The total height of the multilevel APR structure is about 120 cm from the bottom of the sea, and the height of each level is 20 cm. In this experiment, coral fragments were transplanted in the upper, middle, and lower level. Coral transplantation experiments were not applied at the top level to prevent physical damage in coral fragments. The experiments were also not implemented in the coral transplantation in the base of APR (level 5) since the surface of the substrate usually covering sediment due to resuspension (Figure 2). At the beginning of November 2018, 120 coral fragments were transplanted on three levels of APR by two fixation methods: vertically and horizontally orientation of the fragments fixing on the surface of substrates and tied to a paired of the nail using cable ties (Figure 3). Cable ties method of coral transplantation has been widely applied and effective technique for attaching Acropora fragments to artificial substrate (William and Miller 2010;Young et al. 2012). Coral fragment stabilization using cable ties was similarly effective to epoxy or cement methods (William and Miller 2010).

documents.snippet:
In order to optimize reef rehabilitation, combining artificial reefs and coral transplantation is recommended (Abelson 2006;Ammar et al. 2013;Cummings et al. 2015). 

Artificial Patch Reefs (APR) is an artificial structure which is applied to rehabilitate coral reef in order to develop shallow water habitat (Munasik et al. 2018). APR is a rehabilitation tool that is designed by multilevel substrates and applied the combination both of coral transplantation and artificial reefs. Acropora spp. is generally considered as a good for candidates for use in coral transplantation or population enhancement project due to their high growth rate and high survivorship of fragments (Lirman et al. 2010;Boch and Morse 2012;Mercado-Molina 2016;Schopmeyer et al. 2017). The application of APR with Acropora transplanted on their substrates is considered contributing to the local conservation of the small island reefs in the near future. In this study, two Acropora species were selected and applied to investigate the suitable method and species selection for reef rehabilitation. Multilevel substrates of APR may provide the hard substrate to facilitate fragment of coral grows in shallow turbid water. However, the information about the effect of multilevel substrates on survival and growth of transplanted corals is limited. This study aims to address the effectiveness of the APR structure to provide the multilevel substrate to facilitate the growth rate and survival of coral fragment.

documents.title: Successful establishment of a coral nursery for active reef restoration in Kavaratti Island, Lakshadweep archipelago
documents.snippet: The coral transplantation on artificial substrates in the shallow lagoon off the Lakshadweep archipelago has shown promising results in establishing a coral nursery, promoting coral growth and providing a habitat for marine life. The establishment of a coral nursery has led to increased fish aggregation, contributing to enhanced biodiversity and ecosystem resilience. These findings highlight the potential of this restoration technique as a valuable tool in reef conservation efforts for vulnerable ecosystems such as those found in the Lakshadweep archipelago. However, the use of artificial substrates instead of transplanting corals directly onto degraded reefs may present certain limitations, such as differences in the ecological interactions between the artificial and natural environments, potential changes in the structural complexity, and the long-term stability and durability of the artificial substrates. Additionally, the artificial substrates may not fully replicate the conditions necessary for the growth and survival of certain coral species. Continued monitoring and research are essential to assess the long-term effectiveness and sustainability of this approach.

Snippet: Next, we examined settlement preferences in relation to material composition by presenting larvae with a choice between lime mortar substrates containing six different inorganic additives (Fig. 3), a combination of additives (dolomite and strontianite), and control substrates. A. palmata larvae exhibited a slight preference for substrates containing quartz sand (p < 0.05 compared to bioactive glass, dolomite, strontianite, and earthenware ceramic; Fig. 5a), and D. labyrinthiformis larvae exhibited a strong preference for substrates containing quartz sand or strontianite (p < 0.001 compared to all other treatments; Fig. 5b). Notably, the earthenware ceramic substrates-commonly used in larval settlement and coral propagation as "frag plugs" and included here as a reference material-had some of the lowest settlement rates for both species. We also observed that A. palmata larvae preferred to settle on the bottoms of substrates while D. labyrinthiformis larvae preferred the substrate tops (Fig. 5).
