snippet.text:
Between February 2022 and May 2023, we conducted a field experiment in the turf zone using live and structurally intact dead coral colonies from two different branching species: Pocillopora eydouxi and Pocillopora verrucosa. All colonies were collected from the surrounding reef and transplanted to the experimental area. Colonies of P. eydouxi (~40-60 cm tall and ~40-70 cm wide) and P. verrucosa (~30-40 cm tall and ~40-60 cm wide) were carefully removed from their bases using a crowbar. To ensure that live and dead coral patches held comparable structural complexities, we brushed the macroalgae off the dead corals with steel wire brushes, exposing branches and simulating recently dead corals. The original resident fish and invertebrates were also carefully moved to a new substrate before transplantation. Each coral was then secured to the substrate with a 10 cm bolt and underwater epoxy. Four experimental blocks (i.e., four replicates) were constructed in the turf zone, each containing two experimental treatments (a live coral patch and a dead coral patch) and a flat reef area (control patch) (Figure 1a-c). 

Treatment patches consisted of four colonies from each coral species, resulting in eight colonies per patch in a total area of approximately 1 m 2 . The patches were spaced ~5 m apart, forming a triangular shape in each replicate block (Figure 1e). The control patch was defined as a 1 m 2 circle on the flat substrate, and a peg was used to mark its center. Experimental blocks were positioned approximately 10 m apart, parallel to the coastline, at a depth of ~5 m. After set-up, the live and dead coral patches held a cluster of Pocillopora spp. colonies up to 5 cm apart and displayed higher vertical rugosity and more holes than the surrounding flat substrate (see Figure 1a-c). Control patches were dominated by the turf matrix but also displayed sparse holes and occasional small colonies. To compare patch habitat conditions over time, we measured live coral cover and height range, counted the number of refuge categories, and visually estimated rugosity, assigning ranks from 1 to 5, with 1 indicating the lowest and 5 the highest values.

documents.snippet: Coral reefs play an important physiological and ecological role in coastal ecosystems such as providing natural breakwatersthat protect shorelines and human settlements from waves and storm. Corals killed by tsunami, waves and storms are often degraded into rubble. This rubble is dynamic, easily shifted by currents and storms, which effectively forms â€˜â€˜killing fieldsâ€™â€™ forcoral juveniles, hindering coral recovery. In order to rehabilitate coral reefs, artificial substrates are used both for coral transplantation and recruitment. Unfortunately, most artificial substrates are expensive and use land-based material such asconcrete/cement-bases. In order to develop a new low-cost artificial substrate that can replace concrete/cement-base as amedia for coral transplantation, modified coral rubble was tested in a pilot study in Seribu Island, Jakarta. Two different nets (nylon and polyethylene) were used to form rubble into a compact shape, stable and strong substrate. The stability of therubble and the complexity of the surface which is created by the net make this substrate suitable for coral transplantation.Additionally, from an economic perspective the nets are very cheap and locally available. In a number of experiments,modified coral rubble successfully replaced the concrete /cement-base as a media for coral transplantation. The coral transplants were growing over time. With this method, we can try to rehabilitate the degraded coral reef destroyed by tsunami or other factors with material that already is available at the site and with less money. However, this approach requires testing at additional sites and for longer periods, to determine the replicability of the results.Key words: cement base, coral, rubble, transplantation

attempts.answer:
Summary recommendation
For a coastal community with no external funding, the most practical and evidence‑supported option is to build durable, locally stabilized blocks from in‑situ rubble or limestone/coral rock, bound with cheap nets or twine to create rough, self‑stabilizing surfaces, and deploy them in groups anchored with rebar into the seabed; then minimize macroalgae and sediment smothering with inexpensive exclusion/caging and periodic cleaning, and use biodegradable or minimally persistent fasteners and ropes for fragment attachment. <cite id="26caaa00-0">Modified coral rubble compacted with locally available nylon or polyethylene nets formed low‑cost, stable transplant blocks that supported coral growth in field trials in Indonesia</cite> <cite id="26caaa00-1">Direct transplantation onto stable substrates accelerates self‑attachment and improves survival; durable materials (e.g., concrete blocks, metal frames, ceramic tiles, PVC frames) are standard because they become part of the reef</cite> <cite id="e10cae4b-1">Where macroalgae is excluded, coral recruit survival averaged 27% versus <5% when macroalgae grew on frames, demonstrating biofouling control as a top priority</cite> <cite id="e10cae4b-3">Coral recruitment on ceramic tiles attached to concrete blocks at the Seychellles was feasible when local materials limited tile complexity, supporting ceramic-on-concrete composite structures under budget constraints</cite>.

Evidence on materials and performance
- Concrete/cement structures: <cite id="26caaa00-1">Cement blocks are widely used to stabilize rubble and provide settlement surfaces for fragments; durability and weight make them suitable in high‑energy areas</cite>. <cite id="0c8dd35a-2">Concrete composition (basalt, limestone, recycled aggregate) did not significantly alter coral recruitment in field deployments when accounting for environment, indicating material choice may matter less than hydrodynamics and exposure</cite>. <cite id="e10cae4b-3">In the Seychelles, ceramic tiles mounted on concrete blocks recruited corals over 6 months with minimal biofouling, and simple anchoring within the reef framework worked when complex structures were unavailable</cite>.
- Ceramic tiles and “rough” surfaces: <cite id="0c8dd35a-3">Compared to ceramic tiles, PVC poles had greater crustose coralline and turf algal cover but fewer coral recruits, highlighting that material and surface exposure shape recruitment; caution is advised when extrapolating results across substrates</cite>. <cite id="26caaa00-0">Rubble compacted with netting created complex, rough surfaces that supported Acropora growth and outpaced concrete/cement bases in pilot tests, likely due to texture, porosity, and local availability</cite>.
- Plastic/PVC/HDPE structures: <cite id="26caaa00-2">PVC modules are anti‑rust, easy to shape, and durable, and have been used to mount Acropora fragments with adhesive; over 7 months, fragments on PVC structures grew and were monitored at 2‑month intervals</cite>. <cite id="0c8dd35a-1">Low‑cost “shell honeycomb” structures (shell‑like lattices) supported 6‑month post‑settlement survival of ~20% at similar cost to lattice plates, and survival did not significantly differ between a plastic shell honeycomb substrate and more complex structures</cite>.
- Metal and shell/bone: <cite id="26caaa00-1">Metal frames and rebar are common, durable, low‑cost elements for transplant frameworks; in a field deployment, rebar and glass bottles were alternated as attachment points on concrete blocks, with fragments fastened by nylon ties, metal wire, or biodegradable hemp rope</cite>. <cite id="26caaa00-3">Stabilizing blocks with rebar into rubble improved in‑place stability and enabled successful fragment attachment across fastener types</cite>. <cite id="26caaa00-0">Locally available shell/coral rubble can be bound with nets to form stable blocks; this approach grew transplanted corals and avoided expensive cement</cite>.
- Macroalgae and sediment control: <cite id="e10cae4b-1">Macroalgae presence reduced coral recruit survival from ~27% in uncaged, clean substrates to ~5% when macroalgae grew on caged structures, quantifying the need for biofouling control</cite>. <cite id="e10cae4b-4">Macroalgae manipulations and post‑settlement assays showed that larval settlement itself was not impaired by macroalgae canopy, but survival dropped sharply after months when macroalgale biomass increased, reinforcing long‑term fouling risk</cite>. <cite id="0c8dd35a-4">Fine terrigenous sediment inhibits settlement of Pocillopora larvae; above ~0.9 mg cm−2 cover, recruitment was zero in lab assays, highlighting the need to minimize suspended/sedimented particulates on settlement surfaces</cite>.

Mechanisms that drive success
- Surface texture and conditioning: <cite id="0c8dd35a-0">Recruiting Acropora preferentially settle on textured surfaces; 3D‑printed tiles with artificial roughness achieved higher settlement than controls, but spat growth was slower without pre‑conditioning biofilm, implying that both physical texture and in situ biological conditioning matter</cite>. <cite id="0c8dd35a-3">Tiles vs PVC poles showed divergent colonization by coralline algae and turf, with tiles better supporting coral recruits, suggesting that material chemistry and microtopography interact with biofilm to favor settlement and early growth</cite>. <cite id="26caaa00-0">Net‑bound rubble increased surface complexity and provided niches that supported coral attachment and growth, outperforming cement bases in pilot tests</cite>.
- Hydrodynamics and fouling exclusion: <cite id="e10cae4b-1">Simple enclosure of blocks/tiles markedly improved recruit survival by suppressing macroalgal growth that otherwise smothered settlers</cite>. <cite id="e10cae4b-2">Five‑month conditioning showed macroalgae accumulated on open plots but not in caged ones; tiles conditioned in caged treatments yielded adequate recruits for settlement assays, demonstrating the efficacy of fouling exclusion</cite>. <cite id="0c8dd35a-4">Keeping terrigenous sediment below inhibitory thresholds is critical; practical measures include siting higher on the reef where resuspension is lower, avoiding muddy bottoms, and physically cleaning settlers/blocks</cite>.
- Durability and integration: <cite id="26caaa00-1">Durability matters because structures become part of the reef; in high‑energy areas, heavier, robust materials (concrete, metal) integrated better, while in lower‑energy settings, more delicate options (e.g., plastic) can suffice</cite>.

Low‑cost implementation playbook (zero external funding)
1) Source and shape substrate locally
- Rubble/limestone/coral rock: <cite id="26caaa00-0">Form loose rubble into compact blocks with locally available nylon or polyethylene nets or twine; the netting adds stability and surface roughness that corals readily recruit to and grow over</cite>. 
- Concrete blocks: <cite id="26caaa00-1">Use inexpensive concrete frames or poured blocks with embedded glass bottles or hollow spaces for fragment pockets; rebar can be added to increase mass and stability</cite>. <cite id="0c8dd35a-2">Concrete composition (basalt, limestone, recycled aggregate) showed similar recruitment in field tests when environmental exposure was accounted for, suggesting modest cost savings are possible by using locally sourced aggregates</cite>.
- Shell honeycomb/lattice: <cite id="0c8dd35a-1">Construct shell‑like lattices (“shell honeycomb”) from bamboo or driftwood tied with rope; this structure supported ~20% 6‑month survival and matched the performance of more complex plastic structures at one‑tenth the cost; biodegradable or plant fiber ties minimize persistent debris</cite>.

2) Stabilize and anchor to prevent toppling
- <cite id="26caaa00-3">Drive rebar into surrounding rubble and tie blocks to the reef matrix; this prevents displacement during monsoons and keeps settlers in place where currents and light are favorable</cite>. 
- <cite id="26caaa00-1">Use biodegradable hemp rope or nylon ties for fragment attachment to bottles, tiles, or rebar; metal wire can be effective but requires careful tightening to avoid girdling</cite>.

3) Reduce biofouling and sediment smothering
- Exclusion cages: <cite id="e10cae4b-1">Surround each block/tile with a 1–2 m mesh cage made from drift nets or bamboo frames covered with old netting to suppress macroalgal growth; survival was ~27% in uncaged, clean substrates versus ~5% when macroalgae grew</cite>. <cite id="e10cae4b-2">Caged structures maintained low macroalgae volume through months of conditioning, preserving recruitment potential</cite>.
- Placement and maintenance: <cite id="0c8dd35a-4">Avoid muddy substrates and deploy structures in clearer, higher‑energy zones where sediment resuspension is minimized; physically scrub settlers and exposed surfaces monthly with brushes or scraping tools to prevent diatom/turf dominance</cite>.

4) Fast‑track settlement with locally acceptable compromises
- Surface conditioning: <cite id="0c8dd35a-0">If possible, roughen clean surfaces (e.g., scratch tiles, embed shells/bones) to mimic natural texture that recruits prefer; even inexpensive 3D printed textured tiles increased settlement, though growth slowed without biofilm conditioning</cite>.
- Hybrid ceramic‑on‑concrete tiles: <cite id="e10cae4b-3">Use small ceramic tiles on concrete blocks where ceramic alone is scarce; this leveraged ceramic’s favorable colonization while using concrete for stability at minimal cost</cite>.
- Macroalgae‑aware outplanting: <cite id="e10cae4b-1">Before attachment, hold fragments on rubble near the site for 24 h to acclimatize; ensure cages and cleaning routines keep fouling below recruitment thresholds</cite>.

When to choose alternatives
- If coral rubble is scarce but shell/bone/teeth are available: <cite id="26caaa00-0">Bind shell fragments with netting to replicate rubble‑like complexity and support growth</cite>. <cite id="26caaa00-1">Mount fragments in shell/bone pockets on metal frames or rebar as durable, self‑stabilizing carriers</cite>.
- If local expertise favors carpentry: <cite id="0c8dd35a-1">Shell honeycomb lattices built from timber and rope are low‑cost and effective</cite>. 
- If persistent, high survival is required and macroalgae is a major issue: <cite id="e10cae4b-1">Use individual cages per block/tile; combine mechanical cleaning with natural predators (e.g., herbivores) to keep macroalgae low</cite>.

Cautions and trade‑offs
- Material durability vs. persistence: <cite id="26caaa00-1">Plastic/PVC structures are easy to work and durable but add persistent litter; biodegradable ties and timed degradation strategies (hemp rope, cut plastic ties) reduce long‑term impact</cite>.
- Hydrodynamics overhead: <cite id="0c8dd35a-2">Topography and exposure dominate outcomes; a spur‑and‑groove design emulates natural coral coverage where concrete armor failed, underscoring the need to tailor geometry to local waves and depth</cite>.
- Uncertainty: <cite id="26caaa00-0">Rubble‑net blocks showed growth over time but require broader, longer‑term testing for replicability</cite>. <cite id="0c8dd35a-3">Comparisons between PVC and ceramic can bias recruitment metrics; site‑specific trials with local materials are advisable</cite>.

Bottom line for zero‑funding communities
Build rough, locally stabilized blocks using in‑situ rubble bound by cheap nets/twine, anchor them with rebar into the seabed, deploy them in groups with macroalgae exclusion/cages and regular cleaning, and attach fragments with biodegradable fasteners; this approach leverages availability, durability, and settlement‑friendly texture while controlling the dominant threat (macroalgae/sediment). If cement is available, combine concrete blocks with ceramic tiles for settlement patches; if plastics are affordable, use them but plan for eventual replacement or decomposition. <cite id="26caaa00-0">Net‑bound rubble supported Acropora growth and replaced cement bases in field trials with minimal cost</cite> <cite id="26caaa00-1">Durable frameworks and stable substrates accelerate self‑attachment and improve survival, especially when adapted to local hydrodynamics</cite> <cite id="e10cae4b-1">Macroalgae control can more than double recruit survival compared to unmanaged blocks</cite> <cite id="0c8dd35a-1">Low‑cost shell honeycomb/lattice structures achieved ~20% 6‑month survival at a fraction of the cost of complex structures</cite> <cite id="e10cae4b-3">Small ceramic tiles on concrete blocks recruited corals effectively under budget constraints</cite>.

Practical starter kit (budget‑efficient)
- Materials: rubble/limestone, driftwood/bamboo, old nets/fishing line, rebar/sticks, biodegradable rope, plastic/cement supplies if available, concrete molds or wooden frames. <cite id="26caaa00-0">Nets and local rubble are cheap and effective</cite> <cite id="26caaa00-1">Rebar and metal frames stabilize structures; biodegradable or hemp fasteners are acceptable</cite>.
- Steps: 
  1) Build 30–50 cm cube blocks from rubble and netting; punch holes or insert bottles for fragment pockets. <cite id="26caaa00-0">Netting compacts rubble into stable, coral‑friendly blocks</cite>.
  2) Anchor arrays in 2×2 m grids with rebar driven into the reef face. <cite id="26caaa00-3">Rebar anchoring prevents displacement</cite>.
  3) Cage each block with 1–3 m of 50–100 mesh bag or net; rotate monthly to maintain light and reduce macroalgae. <cite id="e10cae4b-1">Caging maintained survival ~27% vs ~5% when macroalgae grew</cite>.
  4) Outplant small lateral branches into net pockets or ceramic tile “microhabitats,” attaching with nylon ties or hemp rope; replace wire ties with rope after 1–2 months to avoid persistent metal. <cite id="26caaa00-3">Fastener options tested successfully; rebar/glass bottle combinations functioned as robust anchors</cite>.
  5) Clean settlers monthly and relocate blocks if sediment/smear accumulates; avoid muddy bottoms. <cite id="0c8dd35a-4">Fine sediment above ~0.9 mg cm−2 eliminated recruitment in lab tests</cite>.

Remaining uncertainties
Head‑to‑head survival of fragments on concrete, ceramic, and net‑bound rubble can vary with site energy and fouling regimes; long‑term, community‑scale trials are needed to rank materials under local hydrodynamics and algal regimes. <cite id="26caaa00-0">Rubble‑net blocks grew corals but need broader, longer replication</cite> <cite id="0c8dd35a-3">Substrate choice biases recruitment and colonization, requiring site‑specific calibration</cite>. A pragmatic path is to run concurrent small trials of: (A) net‑rubble blocks with macroalgae barriers; (B) ceramic tiles on concrete frames with cages; (C) a low‑cost shell honeycomb lattice—monitor survival and growth quarterly and scale to the most cost‑effective option. <cite id="0c8dd35a-1">Shell honeycomb lattices achieved ~20% 6‑month survival with half the material cost of complex structures</cite> <cite id="e10cae4b-1">Macroalgae control can be decisive for survival</cite>.

Title: The Art of Sticking: Attaching Methods Affect Direct Transplantation Success
Snippet: Marine ecosystems such as coral reefs are experiencing a rapid decline in the Anthropocene (Hughes et al. 2017) due to human-induced disturbances and natural phenomena such as hurricanes or monsoon periods (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2007;Hughes et al. 2003). Different approaches, like those used to recover damaged forests, have been attempted to rehabilitate degraded coral reefs over the past few decades abbreviated as "DT") involves attaching coral fragments from a donor to a recipient reef, and these are either attached to artificial structures (Fadli et al. 2012;Williams et al. 2019) or directly transplanted to the substrate (Forrester et al. 2012;Ladd et al. 2019;Lohr et al. 2017). Artificial structures are commonly used to increase coral cover by being deployed in damaged areas with abundant unconsolidated substrate, such as rubble patches (Fadli 2009;Ceccarelli et al. 2020). These include bamboo structures (Ferse 2010), metal frames (Bowden-Kerby 2001;Mahmoud et al. 2019), cement blocks (Chen et al. 2018), ceramic tiles (Forsman et al. 2015), giant clam valves (Dizon et al. 2008;Guest et al. 2011) or PVC frames (Abdo and Hegazy 2015), among others. The use of concrete structures has emerged aiming at either combining substrate stabilization with the provision of habitat structure or providing structure only (Ceccarelli et al. 2020;Razak et al. 2022). When performing a DT approach, it is crucial to use durable materials since they will become a part of the reef (Bowden-Kerby 1997;Lindahl 2003;Dizon et al. 2008). In areas subjected to extreme weather events, it is particularly important to use materials adapted to these conditions. Moreover, applying DT practices on stable substrates can accelerate their self-attachment rates, thus increasing their survival rates (Bowden-Kerby 1997; Edwards and Clark 1999;Lindahl 2003;Dizon and Yap 2006).

Title: Development of Artificial Reefs Using Environmentally Safe Ceramic Material
Snippet: The development of artificial fish reefs has been studied worldwide to enhance fish abundance and diversity, recover coastal and marine habitats, and restore damaged coral reefs [1][2][3][4][5]. Various materials have been used in the construction of artificial reefs worldwide. They include bamboo, concrete blocks, ceramic structures, fibre glass, pipes, reinforced plastic, metal, and marine alloys [6]. Every material, however, has some drawbacks when used as artificial reefs. Bamboo and wood are easily scattered by water currents, lose their fish-aggregating integrity, and cause further degradation of the sea bed [7]. Concrete blocks are durable and can be structured in various configurations, but have limited applications because of their cost [7]. In fact, placing any type of material in the marine environment poses a risk of causing pollution, which would have harmful effects on marine ecosystems [7]. Therefore, by considering detrimental effects apart from benefits, it is necessary to choose materials that have minimal negative impacts on marine environments and can enhance fish colonization. In this regard, ceramic materials are one of the best candidates, because they are economical, environmentally safe, and suitable for hostile marine environments. Santos et al. [8] studied the fish colonization of artificial reefs made of ceramic, concrete, and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) pipes, and they found that ceramic reefs were more effectively colonized than concrete and PVC reefs. Although there have been some studies on the colonization of fish in ceramic reefs, few studies have shown effective reef design and functionality of ceramic materials in a shallow sea environment. 

In this research, ceramic artificial reefs with a hexagonal column structure were designed from a ceramic material. They would be set on sandy sea beds to obtain hard and flat sea beds. The effectiveness of the hexagonal structure was investigated by determining the mechanical strength of the reefs and their sustainability in an adverse shallow sea environment. Ceramic materials were analyzed by measuring chemical constituents, surface texture, water absorption, erosion rate, and durability. These qualities were compared with those of natural coral rubbles.

Title: Macroalgae Inhibits Larval Settlement and Increases Recruit Mortality at Ningaloo Reef, Western Australia
Snippet: Macroalgae in cages. Title: Macroalgae Inhibits Larval Settlement and Increases Recruit Mortality at Ningaloo Reef, Western Australia
Snippet: Manipulating macroalgal biomass. For the post settlement experiment cages, cage controls and uncaged plots were used similar to described for the larval settlement experiment. There were a minimum of three replicates per treatment. The volume of macroalgae in the treatments was assessed when cages were constructed in October 2004, again five months later when the settlement tiles were introduced (March 2005) and thereafter every three months until the conclusion of the experiment in December 2005. 

Coral recruitment and benthic community assessment. Settlement tiles were conditioned in the different caging treatments (caged, uncaged and partial cage) for five months before being seeded with Acropora millepora recruits. Whilst some macroalgae had developed on the settlement tiles, the majority was attached to the reef benthos within the treatments. To remove the potential effects of macroalgal canopy on coral settlement, and ensure there were adequate densities of recruits for the long term experiment, all tiles were removed from the different treatments for larval settlement and placed in benthic chambers on the ocean floor for coral seeding. The tiles were not cleaned so any benthic communities on the tiles which had developed over the five month period were undamaged. The chambers were rectangular containers (20 L volume) with large openings cut out of the sides and lid, which were sealed with 250 μm plankton mesh to permit water exchange but prevent the larvae from escaping. Five tiles were placed in each container in a horizontal position (as per previous conditioning) on a stainless steel screw, so that each tile was raised approximately 2 cm above the bottom of the container. Approximately 3,000 Acropora millepora larvae were injected into the containers, so approximately 600 larvae were available to settle per tile. After two days, the tiles were returned to their original field treatments of caged, uncaged and partially caged plots. Two tiles were placed in each replicate treatment. 

The growth and survival of the A. millepora recruits was assessed by removing the tiles from the field and taking them to a field laboratory for examination under a microscope in a bath of seawater. The first assessment of coral recruits on the settlement tiles was ten days after the tiles were introduced to the cages.

Title: Large-scale coral reef restoration could assist natural recovery in Seychelles, Indian Ocean
Snippet: We deployed settlement tiles onto the reef between 9 th and 15 th January 2014, over 14 months after first coral transplantation. Coral recruitment (spat <1 cm) was compared among all three study sites over a six-month period using settlement tiles. Two ceramic tiles (16 × 16 × 0.8 cm) were placed separately on a concrete block and secured with a plastic cable tie. Flat ceramic tiles attached to concrete blocks were used, rather than other more efficient coral settlement methods (e.g. tiles of differing texture and orientation; Petersen et al. 2005), due to the difficulty of sourcing local materials for more complex settlement structures. Although the results could provide an underestimate of total coral recruitment rates, we considered tile placement appropriate for our objectives. In January 2014, 20 concrete blocks, with two tiles per block, were deployed at each of the three study sites. All concrete blocks were deployed within the same depth range (8-10 m) with adjacent blocks separated by 5 m. This deployment setup resulted in comparable survey areas (ca. 0.12 ha) at each site despite the transplanted site being larger. Families of newly settled corals were identified following Babcock et al. (2003). Title: 3D printed objects do not impact the behavior of a coral-associated damselfish or survival of a settling stony coral
Snippet: Thus, it is important to understand how the survivorship of coral spat may be affected if they settle on 3D printed materials intended for use as settlement sites on natural reefs. Under controlled conditions, P. astreoides chose to settle significantly more in aquaria containing 3D printed tiles compared to control aquaria with no tiles. This result suggests the 3D printed tiles were successfully designed to provide a textured surface that recruiting corals have shown to prefer [29]. While it was not in the scope of the current study to broadly compare settlement rates on 3D printed tiles to more traditional settlement surfaces, this assessment would be valuable for exploring potential alternatives to conventional methodologies. Settlement time for most treatments was comparable to settlement rates observed on more commonly used materials. In a similar experimental design, the settlement rate of P. astreoides on limestone tiles, pre-conditioned in situ, was 12.5% (± 4.95) after a one-week settlement period [30]. After one week in the current study, all treatments had a higher settlement rate on the 3D printed tiles. This is especially significant as the 3D printed treatment tiles were not pre-conditioned with a surface biofilm known to induce settlement and metamorphosis in recruiting corals [31]. However, the mean growth rates of spat on the 3D printed tile treatments were more than 50% lower than P. astreoides settled onto pre-conditioned limestone tiles. As spat growth rate has been shown to be inversely proportional to mortality risk [32], a slow growth rate could have significant implications for juvenile survivorship. Future experiments should consider pre-conditioning 3D printed tiles to differentiate how spat growth is impacted by the presence of a biofilm and the material. 

Percent mortality of corals settled on treatment tiles was comparable to rates observed for P. astreoides in other studies. On conditioned limestone tiles, survival of P. astreoides spat settled under controlled conditions was 10% after 24 hours in situ [33]. After 12 weeks in the current study, survival ranged from 21% (nGen) to 48% (SS). While the rate of survival for P. astreoides settled on 3D printed tiles under controlled conditions is higher than the rates found in other studies, it is likely that mortality would increase if tracked in situ.

Title: ECOLOGICAL ENGINEERING CONSIDERATIONS FOR CORAL REEFS IN THE DESIGN OF MULTIFUNCTIONAL COASTAL STRUCTURES
Snippet: A multifunctional structure is being designed for the Kahului Harbor, Maui, Hawai‘i, to mitigate operational problems caused by wave energy while also providing coral reef habitat. There is limited information on how the design of a coastal structure can be manipulated to enhance the ecology of targeted coral communities. To inform the ecological engineering of an artificial coral reef, the relationship between substrate characteristics and coral colonization was investigated through coral recruitment experiments and study of field conditions. Three concrete compositions that differed by the use of basalt, limestone, or recycled aggregates were tested in field and laboratory experiments to determine the impact of each substrate on the recruitment of juvenile hermatypic corals. The concrete test plates were deployed in three environments for a period of about one year, after which the coral recruits on each plate were identified and counted. No significant difference was found in the average number of coral recruits on the concrete mixed with basalt, limestone and recycled aggregate (60 ± 9, 83 ± 17 and 77 ± 14, respectively). Significant differences in coral recruitment were found due to the laboratory tanks, deep water, and shallow water field tests environments (86 ± 11, 135 ± 15 and 4 ± 1, respectively). These results highlight the importance of environmental site conditions for the development of coral reef habitat. A field study was conducted in the vicinity of purposed artificial reef site to relate the topographic features of the surrounding environment to the levels of live coral coverage. The benthic zone was surveyed using a drop camera system and by divers who recorded in-situ observations. Of the area surveyed, the highest density of coral coverage (>90% cover on 60% of the area) was found on an adjacent natural reef area that was characterized by spur and groove geomorphology with a high degree of macro- and microtopographic complexity. In contrast, sparse coral cover was discovered on the concrete armor units of the existing east breakwater structure, while no live coral cover was observed on the sand and carbonate rubble substrate at the proposed artificial reef location. The high degree of coral coverage on the adjacent natural reef suggests that the artificial coral reef design should emulate the natural spur and groove structure with regards to topographic complexity on multiple scales, orientation with wave direction, and water depth.
</snippet>

Title: A comparison of epibenthic reef communities settling on commonly used experimental substrates: PVC versus ceramic tiles
Snippet: Artificial substrates are routinely used in coral reef research to model the recruitment and growth responses of benthic organisms (e.g. coral recruitment and encrusting organisms) to environmental change. Two commonly used, but structurally different, artificial substrates include cylindrical PVC pipes and flat ceramic tiles. Various ecosystem based models extrapolate data from these substrates interchangeably based on the assumption that results are directly comparable. In order to test this assumption we deployed these commonly used artificial substrate materials, PVC poles and ceramic tiles, in shallow patch reefs for 34 months at One Tree Island, Great Barrier Reef. Tiles were positioned to mimic upwards facing, well-lit substrates (exposed), and downwards facing, shaded (cryptic) substrates. Multivariate analyses demonstrated that the community composition differed significantly between all three treatments. The majority of artificial substrate, coral reef experiments focus on key groups of calcifying organisms, primarily: coralline algae, scleractinian coral and/or total calcareous encruster cover. Interestingly, significant differences in the recruitment, colonisation and community composition of these organisms were detected for our three treatments. When compared to ceramic tiles, PVC poles had greater coverage of crustose coralline algae but reduced levels of coral recruits (< 1 mm diameter) and turf algae. We suggest that comparisons between studies that utilise data from different substrate types should be used with caution. Additionally, large scale modelling and forecasting exercises utilising these data sets should adjust for the inherent biases of each method.
</snippet>

Title: Effects of terrigenous sediment on settlement and survival of the reef coral Pocillopora damicornis
Snippet: Survival and settlement of Pocillopora damicornis larvae on hard surfaces covered with fine (<63 µm) terrigenous red clay was measured in laboratory Petri dishes. The dishes were prepared with sediment films of various thicknesses covering the bottoms. Coral larvae were incubated in the dishes for two weeks and the percent that settled on the bottom was determined. There was a statistically significant relationship between the amount of sediment and coral recruitment on the bottom, with no recruitment on surfaces having a sediment cover above 0.9 mg cm−2. Experimental conditions for the delicate coral larvae were favorable in these experiments. Total survival over the two week settlement tests expressed as the sum of coral recruits and live larvae at the end of the experiment did not show a significant decline, so the major impact of the sediment was on successful settlement rather than on mortality. Larval substrate selection behavior was the primary factor in the observed result.

Summary recommendation
For a coastal community with no external funding, the most practical and evidence‑supported option is to build durable, locally stabilized blocks from in‑situ rubble or limestone/coral rock, bound with cheap nets or twine to create rough, self‑stabilizing surfaces, and deploy them in groups anchored with rebar into the seabed; then minimize macroalgae and sediment smothering with inexpensive exclusion/caging and periodic cleaning, and use biodegradable or minimally persistent fasteners and ropes for fragment attachment. <cite id="26caaa00-0">Modified coral rubble compacted with locally available nylon or polyethylene nets formed low‑cost, stable transplant blocks that supported coral growth in field trials in Indonesia</cite> <cite id="26caaa00-1">Direct transplantation onto stable substrates accelerates self‑attachment and improves survival; durable materials (e.g., concrete blocks, metal frames, ceramic tiles, PVC frames) are standard because they become part of the reef</cite> <cite id="e10cae4b-1">Where macroalgae is excluded, coral recruit survival averaged 27% versus <5% when macroalgae grew on frames, demonstrating biofouling control as a top priority</cite> <cite id="e10cae4b-3">Coral recruitment on ceramic tiles attached to concrete blocks at the Seychellles was feasible when local materials limited tile complexity, supporting ceramic-on-concrete composite structures under budget constraints</cite>.

Evidence on materials and performance
- Concrete/cement structures: <cite id="26caaa00-1">Cement blocks are widely used to stabilize rubble and provide settlement surfaces for fragments; durability and weight make them suitable in high‑energy areas</cite>. <cite id="0c8dd35a-2">Concrete composition (basalt, limestone, recycled aggregate) did not significantly alter coral recruitment in field deployments when accounting for environment, indicating material choice may matter less than hydrodynamics and exposure</cite>. <cite id="e10cae4b-3">In the Seychelles, ceramic tiles mounted on concrete blocks recruited corals over 6 months with minimal biofouling, and simple anchoring within the reef framework worked when complex structures were unavailable</cite>.
- Ceramic tiles and “rough” surfaces: <cite id="0c8dd35a-3">Compared to ceramic tiles, PVC poles had greater crustose coralline and turf algal cover but fewer coral recruits, highlighting that material and surface exposure shape recruitment; caution is advised when extrapolating results across substrates</cite>. <cite id="26caaa00-0">Rubble compacted with netting created complex, rough surfaces that supported Acropora growth and outpaced concrete/cement bases in pilot tests, likely due to texture, porosity, and local availability</cite>.
- Plastic/PVC/HDPE structures: <cite id="26caaa00-2">PVC modules are anti‑rust, easy to shape, and durable, and have been used to mount Acropora fragments with adhesive; over 7 months, fragments on PVC structures grew and were monitored at 2‑month intervals</cite>. <cite id="0c8dd35a-1">Low‑cost “shell honeycomb” structures (shell‑like lattices) supported 6‑month post‑settlement survival of ~20% at similar cost to lattice plates, and survival did not significantly differ between a plastic shell honeycomb substrate and more complex structures</cite>.
- Metal and shell/bone: <cite id="26caaa00-1">Metal frames and rebar are common, durable, low‑cost elements for transplant frameworks; in a field deployment, rebar and glass bottles were alternated as attachment points on concrete blocks, with fragments fastened by nylon ties, metal wire, or biodegradable hemp rope</cite>. <cite id="26caaa00-3">Stabilizing blocks with rebar into rubble improved in‑place stability and enabled successful fragment attachment across fastener types</cite>. <cite id="26caaa00-0">Locally available shell/coral rubble can be bound with nets to form stable blocks; this approach grew transplanted corals and avoided expensive cement</cite>.
- Macroalgae and sediment control: <cite id="e10cae4b-1">Macroalgae presence reduced coral recruit survival from ~27% in uncaged, clean substrates to ~5% when macroalgae grew on caged structures, quantifying the need for biofouling control</cite>. <cite id="e10cae4b-4">Macroalgae manipulations and post‑settlement assays showed that larval settlement itself was not impaired by macroalgae canopy, but survival dropped sharply after months when macroalgale biomass increased, reinforcing long‑term fouling risk</cite>. <cite id="0c8dd35a-4">Fine terrigenous sediment inhibits settlement of Pocillopora larvae; above ~0.9 mg cm−2 cover, recruitment was zero in lab assays, highlighting the need to minimize suspended/sedimented particulates on settlement surfaces</cite>.

Mechanisms that drive success
- Surface texture and conditioning: <cite id="0c8dd35a-0">Recruiting Acropora preferentially settle on textured surfaces; 3D‑printed tiles with artificial roughness achieved higher settlement than controls, but spat growth was slower without pre‑conditioning biofilm, implying that both physical texture and in situ biological conditioning matter</cite>. <cite id="0c8dd35a-3">Tiles vs PVC poles showed divergent colonization by coralline algae and turf, with tiles better supporting coral recruits, suggesting that material chemistry and microtopography interact with biofilm to favor settlement and early growth</cite>. <cite id="26caaa00-0">Net‑bound rubble increased surface complexity and provided niches that supported coral attachment and growth, outperforming cement bases in pilot tests</cite>.
- Hydrodynamics and fouling exclusion: <cite id="e10cae4b-1">Simple enclosure of blocks/tiles markedly improved recruit survival by suppressing macroalgal growth that otherwise smothered settlers</cite>. <cite id="e10cae4b-2">Five‑month conditioning showed macroalgae accumulated on open plots but not in caged ones; tiles conditioned in caged treatments yielded adequate recruits for settlement assays, demonstrating the efficacy of fouling exclusion</cite>. <cite id="0c8dd35a-4">Keeping terrigenous sediment below inhibitory thresholds is critical; practical measures include siting higher on the reef where resuspension is lower, avoiding muddy bottoms, and physically cleaning settlers/blocks</cite>.
- Durability and integration: <cite id="26caaa00-1">Durability matters because structures become part of the reef; in high‑energy areas, heavier, robust materials (concrete, metal) integrated better, while in lower‑energy settings, more delicate options (e.g., plastic) can suffice</cite>.

Low‑cost implementation playbook (zero external funding)
1) Source and shape substrate locally
- Rubble/limestone/coral rock: <cite id="26caaa00-0">Form loose rubble into compact blocks with locally available nylon or polyethylene nets or twine; the netting adds stability and surface roughness that corals readily recruit to and grow over</cite>. 
- Concrete blocks: <cite id="26caaa00-1">Use inexpensive concrete frames or poured blocks with embedded glass bottles or hollow spaces for fragment pockets; rebar can be added to increase mass and stability</cite>. <cite id="0c8dd35a-2">Concrete composition (basalt, limestone, recycled aggregate) showed similar recruitment in field tests when environmental exposure was accounted for, suggesting modest cost savings are possible by using locally sourced aggregates</cite>.
- Shell honeycomb/lattice: <cite id="0c8dd35a-1">Construct shell‑like lattices (“shell honeycomb”) from bamboo or driftwood tied with rope; this structure supported ~20% 6‑month survival and matched the performance of more complex plastic structures at one‑tenth the cost; biodegradable or plant fiber ties minimize persistent debris</cite>.

2) Stabilize and anchor to prevent toppling
- <cite id="26caaa00-3">Drive rebar into surrounding rubble and tie blocks to the reef matrix; this prevents displacement during monsoons and keeps settlers in place where currents and light are favorable</cite>. 
- <cite id="26caaa00-1">Use biodegradable hemp rope or nylon ties for fragment attachment to bottles, tiles, or rebar; metal wire can be effective but requires careful tightening to avoid girdling</cite>.

3) Reduce biofouling and sediment smothering
- Exclusion cages: <cite id="e10cae4b-1">Surround each block/tile with a 1–2 m mesh cage made from drift nets or bamboo frames covered with old netting to suppress macroalgal growth; survival was ~27% in uncaged, clean substrates versus ~5% when macroalgae grew</cite>. <cite id="e10cae4b-2">Caged structures maintained low macroalgae volume through months of conditioning, preserving recruitment potential</cite>.
- Placement and maintenance: <cite id="0c8dd35a-4">Avoid muddy substrates and deploy structures in clearer, higher‑energy zones where sediment resuspension is minimized; physically scrub settlers and exposed surfaces monthly with brushes or scraping tools to prevent diatom/turf dominance</cite>.

4) Fast‑track settlement with locally acceptable compromises
- Surface conditioning: <cite id="0c8dd35a-0">If possible, roughen clean surfaces (e.g., scratch tiles, embed shells/bones) to mimic natural texture that recruits prefer; even inexpensive 3D printed textured tiles increased settlement, though growth slowed without biofilm conditioning</cite>.
- Hybrid ceramic‑on‑concrete tiles: <cite id="e10cae4b-3">Use small ceramic tiles on concrete blocks where ceramic alone is scarce; this leveraged ceramic’s favorable colonization while using concrete for stability at minimal cost</cite>.
- Macroalgae‑aware outplanting: <cite id="e10cae4b-1">Before attachment, hold fragments on rubble near the site for 24 h to acclimatize; ensure cages and cleaning routines keep fouling below recruitment thresholds</cite>.

When to choose alternatives
- If coral rubble is scarce but shell/bone/teeth are available: <cite id="26caaa00-0">Bind shell fragments with netting to replicate rubble‑like complexity and support growth</cite>. <cite id="26caaa00-1">Mount fragments in shell/bone pockets on metal frames or rebar as durable, self‑stabilizing carriers</cite>.
- If local expertise favors carpentry: <cite id="0c8dd35a-1">Shell honeycomb lattices built from timber and rope are low‑cost and effective</cite>. 
- If persistent, high survival is required and macroalgae is a major issue: <cite id="e10cae4b-1">Use individual cages per block/tile; combine mechanical cleaning with natural predators (e.g., herbivores) to keep macroalgae low</cite>.

Cautions and trade‑offs
- Material durability vs. persistence: <cite id="26caaa00-1">Plastic/PVC structures are easy to work and durable but add persistent litter; biodegradable ties and timed degradation strategies (hemp rope, cut plastic ties) reduce long‑term impact</cite>.
- Hydrodynamics overhead: <cite id="0c8dd35a-2">Topography and exposure dominate outcomes; a spur‑and‑groove design emulates natural coral coverage where concrete armor failed, underscoring the need to tailor geometry to local waves and depth</cite>.
- Uncertainty: <cite id="26caaa00-0">Rubble‑net blocks showed growth over time but require broader, longer‑term testing for replicability</cite>. <cite id="0c8dd35a-3">Comparisons between PVC and ceramic can bias recruitment metrics; site‑specific trials with local materials are advisable</cite>.

Bottom line for zero‑funding communities
Build rough, locally stabilized blocks using in‑situ rubble bound by cheap nets/twine, anchor them with rebar into the seabed, deploy them in groups with macroalgae exclusion/cages and regular cleaning, and attach fragments with biodegradable fasteners; this approach leverages availability, durability, and settlement‑friendly texture while controlling the dominant threat (macroalgae/sediment). If cement is available, combine concrete blocks with ceramic tiles for settlement patches; if plastics are affordable, use them but plan for eventual replacement or decomposition. <cite id="26caaa00-0">Net‑bound rubble supported Acropora growth and replaced cement bases in field trials with minimal cost</cite> <cite id="26caaa00-1">Durable frameworks and stable substrates accelerate self‑attachment and improve survival, especially when adapted to local hydrodynamics</cite> <cite id="e10cae4b-1">Macroalgae control can more than double recruit survival compared to unmanaged blocks</cite> <cite id="0c8dd35a-1">Low‑cost shell honeycomb/lattice structures achieved ~20% 6‑month survival at a fraction of the cost of complex structures</cite> <cite id="e10cae4b-3">Small ceramic tiles on concrete blocks recruited corals effectively under budget constraints</cite>.

Practical starter kit (budget‑efficient)
- Materials: rubble/limestone, driftwood/bamboo, old nets/fishing line, rebar/sticks, biodegradable rope, plastic/cement supplies if available, concrete molds or wooden frames. <cite id="26caaa00-0">Nets and local rubble are cheap and effective</cite> <cite id="26caaa00-1">Rebar and metal frames stabilize structures; biodegradable or hemp fasteners are acceptable</cite>.
- Steps: 
  1) Build 30–50 cm cube blocks from rubble and netting; punch holes or insert bottles for fragment pockets. <cite id="26caaa00-0">Netting compacts rubble into stable, coral‑friendly blocks</cite>.
  2) Anchor arrays in 2×2 m grids with rebar driven into the reef face. <cite id="26caaa00-3">Rebar anchoring prevents displacement</cite>.
  3) Cage each block with 1–3 m of 50–100 mesh bag or net; rotate monthly to maintain light and reduce macroalgae. <cite id="e10cae4b-1">Caging maintained survival ~27% vs ~5% when macroalgae grew</cite>.
  4) Outplant small lateral branches into net pockets or ceramic tile “microhabitats,” attaching with nylon ties or hemp rope; replace wire ties with rope after 1–2 months to avoid persistent metal. <cite id="26caaa00-3">Fastener options tested successfully; rebar/glass bottle combinations functioned as robust anchors</cite>.
  5) Clean settlers monthly and relocate blocks if sediment/smear accumulates; avoid muddy bottoms. <cite id="0c8dd35a-4">Fine sediment above ~0.9 mg cm−2 eliminated recruitment in lab tests</cite>.

Remaining uncertainties
Head‑to‑head survival of fragments on concrete, ceramic, and net‑bound rubble can vary with site energy and fouling regimes; long‑term, community‑scale trials are needed to rank materials under local hydrodynamics and algal regimes. <cite id="26caaa00-0">Rubble‑net blocks grew corals but need broader, longer replication</cite> <cite id="0c8dd35a-3">Substrate choice biases recruitment and colonization, requiring site‑specific calibration</cite>. A pragmatic path is to run concurrent small trials of: (A) net‑rubble blocks with macroalgae barriers; (B) ceramic tiles on concrete frames with cages; (C) a low‑cost shell honeycomb lattice—monitor survival and growth quarterly and scale to the most cost‑effective option. <cite id="0c8dd35a-1">Shell honeycomb lattices achieved ~20% 6‑month survival with half the material cost of complex structures</cite> <cite id="e10cae4b-1">Macroalgae control can be decisive for survival</cite>.
</answer>

Title: The Art of Sticking: Attaching Methods Affect Direct Transplantation Success

Before being transplanted, we allocated these fragments on a rubble patch close to the rehabilitation site for 24 h to reduce possible stress produced during the collection (Forrester et al. 2012).

Title: Development of Artificial Reefs Using Environmentally Safe Ceramic Material

In fact, placing any type of material in the marine environment poses a risk of causing pollution, which would have harmful effects on marine ecosystems [7]. snippet.text: Coral reefs play an important physiological and ecological role in coastal ecosystems such as providing natural breakwatersthat protect shorelines and human settlements from waves and storm. Corals killed by tsunami, waves and storms are often degraded into rubble. This rubble is dynamic, easily shifted by currents and storms, which effectively forms â€˜â€˜killing fieldsâ€™â€™ forcoral juveniles, hindering coral recovery. In order to rehabilitate coral reefs, artificial substrates are used both for coral transplantation and recruitment. Unfortunately, most artificial substrates are expensive and use land-based material such asconcrete/cement-bases. In order to develop a new low-cost artificial substrate that can replace concrete/cement-base as amedia for coral transplantation, modified coral rubble was tested in a pilot study in Seribu Island, Jakarta. Two different nets (nylon and polyethylene) were used to form rubble into a compact shape, stable and strong substrate. The stability of therubble and the complexity of the surface which is created by the net make this substrate suitable for coral transplantation.Additionally, from an economic perspective the nets are very cheap and locally available. In a number of experiments,modified coral rubble successfully replaced the concrete /cement-base as a media for coral transplantation. The coral transplants were growing over time. snippet.text: Marine ecosystems such as coral reefs are experiencing a rapid decline in the Anthropocene (Hughes et al. 2017) due to human-induced disturbances and natural phenomena such as hurricanes or monsoon periods (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2007;Hughes et al. 2003). Different approaches, like those used to recover damaged forests, have been attempted to rehabilitate degraded coral reefs over the past few decades abbreviated as "DT") involves attaching coral fragments from a donor to a recipient reef, and these are either attached to artificial structures (Fadli et al. 2012;Williams et al. 2019) or directly transplanted to the substrate (Forrester et al. 2012;Ladd et al. 2019;Lohr et al. 2017). Artificial structures are commonly used to increase coral cover by being deployed in damaged areas with abundant unconsolidated substrate, such as rubble patches (Fadli 2009;Ceccarelli et al. 2020). These include bamboo structures (Ferse 2010), metal frames (Bowden-Kerby 2001;Mahmoud et al. 2019), cement blocks (Chen et al. 2018), ceramic tiles (Forsman et al. 2015), giant clam valves (Dizon et al. 2008;Guest et al. 2011) or PVC frames (Abdo and Hegazy 2015), among others. The use of concrete structures has emerged aiming at either combining substrate stabilization with the provision of habitat structure or providing structure only (Ceccarelli et al. 2020;Razak et al. 2022). When performing a DT approach, it is crucial to use durable materials since they will become a part of the reef (Bowden-Kerby 1997;Lindahl 2003;Dizon et al. 2008). In areas subjected to extreme weather events, it is particularly important to use materials adapted to these conditions. Moreover, applying DT practices on stable substrates can accelerate their self-attachment rates, thus increasing their survival rates (Bowden-Kerby 1997; Edwards and Clark 1999;Lindahl 2003;Dizon and Yap 2006).

Title: Macroalgae Inhibits Larval Settlement and Increases Recruit Mortality at Ningaloo Reef, Western Australia
Snippet: Macroalgae in cages. The mean volume of macroalgae increased significantly in the caged plots through time, but remained low in the uncaged and partially caged plots (Fig 2 , Table 1 and S5 Table ). The mean volume in the cages was highest after six months due to the seasonal growth of Hydroclathrus clathratus, which disappeared almost completely during the subsequent three months. At the conclusion of the experiment the caged treatments were dominated by the bushy upright Sargassum spp. and Dictyota cervicornis. 

Benthic cover on settlement tiles. In the post-settlement experiment the benthic cover on the underside of tiles was assessed at the start of the experiment, immediately prior to the tiles being seeded by coral larvae. The main benthic cover was bare "bare" (covered with a biofilm of diatoms) and turf algae (S6 Table ). There were no significant differences in the benthic cover on the tiles between the caged, uncaged and partially caged treatments (PERMANOVA F = 0.96, p = 0.47, S7 Table ). 

Larval settlement. The total number of corals present on the underside of tiles at the start of the post-settlement experiment did not differ significantly among treatments (F = 1.05, p = 0.38, S8 Table ). There was an average of 57.2 ± 11.3 S.E coral recruits per tile at the start of the experiment. The majority of corals settled to the undersurface of the tiles (S9 Table ) and there were no significant differences in the proportion of corals settling to the different tiles surfaces between treatments (F = 0.78, p < 0.54, S10 Table ) Coral recruit survival. Over the nine month period, the number of surviving corals decreased in all treatments, however, the survival was much lower in the caged treatments compared to the uncaged treatments and cage controls (Fig 3). By the conclusion of the experiment the percentage of surviving corals was on average, 5.7 + 1.7 S.E. % in the caged treatments compared to 27.1 + 4.6 S.E. % in the uncaged treatments.

Title: Macroalgae Inhibits Larval Settlement and Increases Recruit Mortality at Ningaloo Reef, Western Australia
Snippet: Manipulating macroalgal biomass. For the post settlement experiment cages, cage controls and uncaged plots were used similar to described for the larval settlement experiment. There were a minimum of three replicates per treatment. The volume of macroalgae in the treatments was assessed when cages were constructed in October 2004, again five months later when the settlement tiles were introduced (March 2005) and thereafter every three months until the conclusion of the experiment in December 2005. 

Coral recruitment and benthic community assessment. Settlement tiles were conditioned in the different caging treatments (caged, uncaged and partial cage) for five months before being seeded with Acropora millepora recruits. Whilst some macroalgae had developed on the settlement tiles, the majority was attached to the reef benthos within the treatments. To remove the potential effects of macroalgal canopy on coral settlement, and ensure there were adequate densities of recruits for the long term experiment, all tiles were removed from the different treatments for larval settlement and placed in benthic chambers on the ocean floor for coral seeding. The tiles were not cleaned so any benthic communities on the tiles which had developed over the five month period were undamaged. The chambers were rectangular containers (20 L volume) with large openings cut out of the sides and lid, which were sealed with 250 μm plankton mesh to permit water exchange but prevent the larvae from escaping. Five tiles were placed in each container in a horizontal position (as per previous conditioning) on a stainless steel screw, so that each tile was raised approximately 2 cm above the bottom of the container. Approximately 3,000 Acropora millepora larvae were injected into the containers, so approximately 600 larvae were available to settle per tile. After two days, the tiles were returned to their original field treatments of caged, uncaged and partially caged plots. Two tiles were placed in each replicate treatment. 

The growth and survival of the A. millepora recruits was assessed by removing the tiles from the field and taking them to a field laboratory for examination under a microscope in a bath of seawater. The first assessment of coral recruits on the settlement tiles was ten days after the tiles were introduced to the cages.

Title: Large-scale coral reef restoration could assist natural recovery in Seychelles, Indian Ocean
Snippet: We deployed settlement tiles onto the reef between 9 th and 15 th January 2014, over 14 months after first coral transplantation. Based on our coral reproduction monitoring, this deployment schedule allowed approximately 3 weeks biological conditioning of the tiles prior to the first expected coral spawning in the area, the first week of February 2014 (Montoya-Maya, unpublished data).

Coral recruitment (spat <1 cm) was compared among all three study sites over a six-month period using settlement tiles. Two ceramic tiles (16 × 16 × 0.8 cm) were placed separately on a concrete block and secured with a plastic cable tie. Flat ceramic tiles attached to concrete blocks were used, rather than other more efficient coral settlement methods (e.g. tiles of differing texture and orientation; Petersen et al. 2005), due to the difficulty of sourcing local materials for more complex settlement structures. Although the results could provide an underestimate of total coral recruitment rates, we considered tile placement appropriate for our objectives. In January 2014, 20 concrete blocks, with two tiles per block, were deployed at each of the three study sites. All concrete blocks were deployed within the same depth range (8-10 m) with adjacent blocks separated by 5 m. This deployment setup resulted in comparable survey areas (ca. 0.12 ha) at each site despite the transplanted site being larger. Tiles were retrieved in July 2014, >19 months after first transplantation. Tiles were left to dry in the sun for 24 hours and then rinsed in freshwater to remove sediments. Biofouling was insignificant and similar across sites, therefore, we considered unnecessary soaking the tiles in diluted bleach. Each tile was then visually examined twice by different observers using a stereomicroscope to identify coral spat. The coral spat were counted and identified to family level. Families of newly settled corals were identified following Babcock et al. (2003). Families that could not be identified due to damage or insufficient development were pooled into the category "unidentified".

There were a minimum of three replicates per treatment. The volume of macroalgae in the treatments was assessed when cages were constructed in October 2004, again five months later when the settlement tiles were introduced (March 2005) and thereafter every three months until the conclusion of the experiment in December 2005. 

Coral recruitment and benthic community assessment. Settlement tiles were conditioned in the different caging treatments (caged, uncaged and partial cage) for five months before being seeded with Acropora millepora recruits. Whilst some macroalgae had developed on the settlement tiles, the majority was attached to the reef benthos within the treatments. To remove the potential effects of macroalgal canopy on coral settlement, and ensure there were adequate densities of recruits for the long term experiment, all tiles were removed from the different treatments for larval settlement and placed in benthic chambers on the ocean floor for coral seeding. The tiles were not cleaned so any benthic communities on the tiles which had developed over the five month period were undamaged. The chambers were rectangular containers (20 L volume) with large openings cut out of the sides and lid, which were sealed with 250 μm plankton mesh to permit water exchange but prevent the larvae from escaping. Five tiles were placed in each container in a horizontal position (as per previous conditioning) on a stainless steel screw, so that each tile was raised approximately 2 cm above the bottom of the container. Approximately 3,000 Acropora millepora larvae were injected into the containers, so approximately 600 larvae were available to settle per tile. After two days, the tiles were returned to their original field treatments of caged, uncaged and partially caged plots. Two tiles were placed in each replicate treatment. 

The growth and survival of the A. millepora recruits was assessed by removing the tiles from the field and taking them to a field laboratory for examination under a microscope in a bath of seawater. snippet.text:
We deployed settlement tiles onto the reef between 9 th and 15 th January 2014, over 14 months after first coral transplantation. Based on our coral reproduction monitoring, this deployment schedule allowed approximately 3 weeks biological conditioning of the tiles prior to the first expected coral spawning in the area, the first week of February 2014 (Montoya-Maya, unpublished data).

Coral recruitment (spat <1 cm) was compared among all three study sites over a six-month period using settlement tiles. Two ceramic tiles (16 × 16 × 0.8 cm) were placed separately on a concrete block and secured with a plastic cable tie. Flat ceramic tiles attached to concrete blocks were used, rather than other more efficient coral settlement methods (e.g. tiles of differing texture and orientation; Petersen et al. 2005), due to the difficulty of sourcing local materials for more complex settlement structures. Although the results could provide an underestimate of total coral recruitment rates, we considered tile placement appropriate for our objectives. In January 2014, 20 concrete blocks, with two tiles per block, were deployed at each of the three study sites. All concrete blocks were deployed within the same depth range (8-10 m) with adjacent blocks separated by 5 m. This deployment setup resulted in comparable survey areas (ca. 0.12 ha) at each site despite the transplanted site being larger. Tiles were retrieved in July 2014, >19 months after first transplantation. Tiles were left to dry in the sun for 24 hours and then rinsed in freshwater to remove sediments. Biofouling was insignificant and similar across sites, therefore, we considered unnecessary soaking the tiles in diluted bleach. Each tile was then visually examined twice by different observers using a stereomicroscope to identify coral spat. The coral spat were counted and identified to family level. Families of newly settled corals were identified following Babcock et al. (2003). Families that could not be identified due to damage or insufficient development were pooled into the category "unidentified".

snippet.text: Marine ecosystems such as coral reefs are experiencing a rapid decline in the Anthropocene (Hughes et al. 2017) due to human-induced disturbances and natural phenomena such as hurricanes or monsoon periods (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2007;Hughes et al. 2003). Different approaches, like those used to recover damaged forests, have been attempted to rehabilitate degraded coral reefs over the past few decades abbreviated as "DT") involves attaching coral fragments from a donor to a recipient reef, and these are either attached to artificial structures (Fadli et al. 2012;Williams et al. 2019) or directly transplanted to the substrate (Forrester et al. 2012;Ladd et al. 2019;Lohr et al. 2017). Artificial structures are commonly used to increase coral cover by being deployed in damaged areas with abundant unconsolidated substrate, such as rubble patches (Fadli 2009;Ceccarelli et al. 2020). These include bamboo structures (Ferse 2010), metal frames (Bowden-Kerby 2001;Mahmoud et al. 2019), cement blocks (Chen et al. 2018), ceramic tiles (Forsman et al. 2015), giant clam valves (Dizon et al. 2008;Guest et al. 2011) or PVC frames (Abdo and Hegazy 2015), among others. The use of concrete structures has emerged aiming at either combining substrate stabilization with the provision of habitat structure or providing structure only (Ceccarelli et al. 2020;Razak et al. 2022). When performing a DT approach, it is crucial to use durable materials since they will become a part of the reef (Bowden-Kerby 1997;Lindahl 2003;Dizon et al. 2008). In areas subjected to extreme weather events, it is particularly important to use materials adapted to these conditions. Moreover, applying DT practices on stable substrates can accelerate their self-attachment rates, thus increasing their survival rates (Bowden-Kerby 1997; Edwards and Clark 1999;Lindahl 2003;Dizon and Yap 2006).

Title: 3D printed objects do not impact the behavior of a coral-associated damselfish or survival of a settling stony coral
Snippet: Thus, it is important to understand how the survivorship of coral spat may be affected if they settle on 3D printed materials intended for use as settlement sites on natural reefs. Under controlled conditions, P. astreoides chose to settle significantly more in aquaria containing 3D printed tiles compared to control aquaria with no tiles. This result suggests the 3D printed tiles were successfully designed to provide a textured surface that recruiting corals have shown to prefer [29]. While it was not in the scope of the current study to broadly compare settlement rates on 3D printed tiles to more traditional settlement surfaces, this assessment would be valuable for exploring potential alternatives to conventional methodologies. Settlement time for most treatments was comparable to settlement rates observed on more commonly used materials. In a similar experimental design, the settlement rate of P. astreoides on limestone tiles, pre-conditioned in situ, was 12.5% (± 4.95) after a one-week settlement period [30]. After one week in the current study, all treatments had a higher settlement rate on the 3D printed tiles. This is especially significant as the 3D printed treatment tiles were not pre-conditioned with a surface biofilm known to induce settlement and metamorphosis in recruiting corals [31]. However, the mean growth rates of spat on the 3D printed tile treatments were more than 50% lower than P. astreoides settled onto pre-conditioned limestone tiles. As spat growth rate has been shown to be inversely proportional to mortality risk [32], a slow growth rate could have significant implications for juvenile survivorship. Future experiments should consider pre-conditioning 3D printed tiles to differentiate how spat growth is impacted by the presence of a biofilm and the material. 

Percent mortality of corals settled on treatment tiles was comparable to rates observed for P. astreoides in other studies. On conditioned limestone tiles, survival of P. astreoides spat settled under controlled conditions was 10% after 24 hours in situ [33]. After 12 weeks in the current study, survival ranged from 21% (nGen) to 48% (SS). While the rate of survival for P. astreoides settled on 3D printed tiles under controlled conditions is higher than the rates found in other studies, it is likely that mortality would increase if tracked in situ.

Title: Enhancing coral larval supply and seedling production using a special bundle collection system “coral larval cradle” for large‐scale coral restoration
Snippet: We demonstrated that the post-settlement survival at 6 months after settlement on lattice plates and SHS was 20% if a bottom-raised rack was used. In other words, settling 10 larvae per plate would be sufficient to support more than one juvenile coral on the plate after 6 months. The cost of pSHS was one-tenth that of the lattice plate, and half of the mSHS substrate in this study. However, due to pollution concerns, the material used for the artificial plate should not be plastic if the mass-produced corals are eventually to be outplanted. When we compared the survival rate of the corals between the pSHS and mSHS substrates over a 6month period, no significant differences were observed, suggesting that the mSHS substrate is suitable for outplanting.

Title: ECOLOGICAL ENGINEERING CONSIDERATIONS FOR CORAL REEFS IN THE DESIGN OF MULTIFUNCTIONAL COASTAL STRUCTURES
Snippet: A multifunctional structure is being designed for the Kahului Harbor, Maui, Hawai‘i, to mitigate operational problems caused by wave energy while also providing coral reef habitat. There is limited information on how the design of a coastal structure can be manipulated to enhance the ecology of targeted coral communities. To inform the ecological engineering of an artificial coral reef, the relationship between substrate characteristics and coral colonization was investigated through coral recruitment experiments and study of field conditions. Three concrete compositions that differed by the use of basalt, limestone, or recycled aggregates were tested in field and laboratory experiments to determine the impact of each substrate on the recruitment of juvenile hermatypic corals. The concrete test plates were deployed in three environments for a period of about one year, after which the coral recruits on each plate were identified and counted. No significant difference was found in the average number of coral recruits on the concrete mixed with basalt, limestone and recycled aggregate (60 ± 9, 83 ± 17 and 77 ± 14, respectively). Significant differences in coral recruitment were found due to the laboratory tanks, deep water, and shallow water field tests environments (86 ± 11, 135 ± 15 and 4 ± 1, respectively). These results highlight the importance of environmental site conditions for the development of coral reef habitat. A field study was conducted in the vicinity of purposed artificial reef site to relate the topographic features of the surrounding environment to the levels of live coral coverage. The benthic zone was surveyed using a drop camera system and by divers who recorded in-situ observations. Of the area surveyed, the highest density of coral coverage (>90% cover on 60% of the area) was found on an adjacent natural reef area that was characterized by spur and groove geomorphology with a high degree of macro- and microtopographic complexity. In contrast, sparse coral cover was discovered on the concrete armor units of the existing east breakwater structure, while no live coral cover was observed on the sand and carbonate rubble substrate at the proposed artificial reef location. The high degree of coral coverage on the adjacent natural reef suggests that the artificial coral reef design should emulate the natural spur and groove structure with regards to topographic complexity on multiple scales, orientation with wave direction, and water depth.

Title: A comparison of epibenthic reef communities settling on commonly used experimental substrates: PVC versus ceramic tiles
Snippet: Artificial substrates are routinely used in coral reef research to model the recruitment and growth responses of benthic organisms (e.g. coral recruitment and encrusting organisms) to environmental change. Two commonly used, but structurally different, artificial substrates include cylindrical PVC pipes and flat ceramic tiles. Various ecosystem based models extrapolate data from these substrates interchangeably based on the assumption that results are directly comparable. In order to test this assumption we deployed these commonly used artificial substrate materials, PVC poles and ceramic tiles, in shallow patch reefs for 34 months at One Tree Island, Great Barrier Reef. Tiles were positioned to mimic upwards facing, well-lit substrates (exposed), and downwards facing, shaded (cryptic) substrates. Multivariate analyses demonstrated that the community composition differed significantly between all three treatments. The majority of artificial substrate, coral reef experiments focus on key groups of calcifying organisms, primarily: coralline algae, scleractinian coral and/or total calcareous encruster cover. Interestingly, significant differences in the recruitment, colonisation and community composition of these organisms were detected for our three treatments. When compared to ceramic tiles, PVC poles had greater coverage of crustose coralline algae but reduced levels of coral recruits (< 1 mm diameter) and turf algae. We suggest that comparisons between studies that utilise data from different substrate types should be used with caution. Additionally, large scale modelling and forecasting exercises utilising these data sets should adjust for the inherent biases of each method.

Title: Effects of terrigenous sediment on settlement and survival of the reef coral Pocillopora damicornis
Snippet: Survival and settlement of Pocillopora damicornis larvae on hard surfaces covered with fine (<63 µm) terrigenous red clay was measured in laboratory Petri dishes. The dishes were prepared with sediment films of various thicknesses covering the bottoms. Coral larvae were incubated in the dishes for two weeks and the percent that settled on the bottom was determined. There was a statistically significant relationship between the amount of sediment and coral recruitment on the bottom, with no recruitment on surfaces having a sediment cover above 0.9 mg cm−2. Experimental conditions for the delicate coral larvae were favorable in these experiments. Total survival over the two week settlement tests expressed as the sum of coral recruits and live larvae at the end of the experiment did not show a significant decline, so the major impact of the sediment was on successful settlement rather than on mortality. Larval substrate selection behavior was the primary factor in the observed result.

snippet.text: A multifunctional structure is being designed for the Kahului Harbor, Maui, Hawai‘i, to mitigate operational problems caused by wave energy while also providing coral reef habitat. There is limited information on how the design of a coastal structure can be manipulated to enhance the ecology of targeted coral communities. To inform the ecological engineering of an artificial coral reef, the relationship between substrate characteristics and coral colonization was investigated through coral recruitment experiments and study of field conditions. Three concrete compositions that differed by the use of basalt, limestone, or recycled aggregates were tested in field and laboratory experiments to determine the impact of each substrate on the recruitment of juvenile hermatypic corals. The concrete test plates were deployed in three environments for a period of about one year, after which the coral recruits on each plate were identified and counted. No significant difference was found in the average number of coral recruits on the concrete mixed with basalt, limestone and recycled aggregate (60 ± 9, 83 ± 17 and 77 ± 14, respectively). Significant differences in coral recruitment were found due to the laboratory tanks, deep water, and shallow water field tests environments (86 ± 11, 135 ± 15 and 4 ± 1, respectively). These results highlight the importance of environmental site conditions for the development of coral reef habitat. A field study was conducted in the vicinity of purposed artificial reef site to relate the topographic features of the surrounding environment to the levels of live coral coverage. The benthic zone was surveyed using a drop camera system and by divers who recorded in-situ observations. Of the area surveyed, the highest density of coral coverage (>90% cover on 60% of the area) was found on an adjacent natural reef area that was characterized by spur and groove geomorphology with a high degree of macro- and microtopographic complexity. In contrast, sparse coral cover was discovered on the concrete armor units of the existing east breakwater structure, while no live coral cover was observed on the sand and carbonate rubble substrate at the proposed artificial reef location. The high degree of coral coverage on the adjacent natural reef suggests that the artificial coral reef design should emulate the natural spur and groove structure with regards to topographic complexity on multiple scales, orientation with wave direction, and water depth.
