snippet.text: Artificial substrates are routinely used in coral reef research to model the recruitment and growth responses of benthic organisms (e.g. coral recruitment and encrusting organisms) to environmental change. Two commonly used, but structurally different, artificial substrates include cylindrical PVC pipes and flat ceramic tiles. Various ecosystem based models extrapolate data from these substrates interchangeably based on the assumption that results are directly comparable. In order to test this assumption we deployed these commonly used artificial substrate materials, PVC poles and ceramic tiles, in shallow patch reefs for 34 months at One Tree Island, Great Barrier Reef. Tiles were positioned to mimic upwards facing, well-lit substrates (exposed), and downwards facing, shaded (cryptic) substrates. Multivariate analyses demonstrated that the community composition differed significantly between all three treatments. The majority of artificial substrate, coral reef experiments focus on key groups of calcifying organisms, primarily: coralline algae, scleractinian coral and/or total calcareous encruster cover. Interestingly, significant differences in the recruitment, colonisation and community composition of these organisms were detected for our three treatments. When compared to ceramic tiles, PVC poles had greater coverage of crustose coralline algae but reduced levels of coral recruits (< 1 mm diameter) and turf algae. We suggest that comparisons between studies that utilise data from different substrate types should be used with caution. Additionally, large scale modelling and forecasting exercises utilising these data sets should adjust for the inherent biases of each method.

snippet.text: Survival and settlement of Pocillopora damicornis larvae on hard surfaces covered with fine (<63 µm) terrigenous red clay was measured in laboratory Petri dishes. The dishes were prepared with sediment films of various thicknesses covering the bottoms. Coral larvae were incubated in the dishes for two weeks and the percent that settled on the bottom was determined. There was a statistically significant relationship between the amount of sediment and coral recruitment on the bottom, with no recruitment on surfaces having a sediment cover above 0.9 mg cm−2. Experimental conditions for the delicate coral larvae were favorable in these experiments. Total survival over the two week settlement tests expressed as the sum of coral recruits and live larvae at the end of the experiment did not show a significant decline, so the major impact of the sediment was on successful settlement rather than on mortality. Larval substrate selection behavior was the primary factor in the observed result.

documents.title: 3D printed objects do not impact the behavior of a coral-associated damselfish or survival of a settling stony coral
documents.snippet:
Thus, it is important to understand how the survivorship of coral spat may be affected if they settle on 3D printed materials intended for use as settlement sites on natural reefs. Under controlled conditions, P. astreoides chose to settle significantly more in aquaria containing 3D printed tiles compared to control aquaria with no tiles. This result suggests the 3D printed tiles were successfully designed to provide a textured surface that recruiting corals have shown to prefer [29]. While it was not in the scope of the current study to broadly compare settlement rates on 3D printed tiles to more traditional settlement surfaces, this assessment would be valuable for exploring potential alternatives to conventional methodologies. Settlement time for most treatments was comparable to settlement rates observed on more commonly used materials. In a similar experimental design, the settlement rate of P. astreoides on limestone tiles, pre-conditioned in situ, was 12.5% (± 4.95) after a one-week settlement period [30]. After one week in the current study, all treatments had a higher settlement rate on the 3D printed tiles. This is especially significant as the 3D printed treatment tiles were not pre-conditioned with a surface biofilm known to induce settlement and metamorphosis in recruiting corals [31]. However, the mean growth rates of spat on the 3D printed tile treatments were more than 50% lower than P. astreoides settled onto pre-conditioned limestone tiles. As spat growth rate has been shown to be inversely proportional to mortality risk [32], a slow growth rate could have significant implications for juvenile survivorship. Future experiments should consider pre-conditioning 3D printed tiles to differentiate how spat growth is impacted by the presence of a biofilm and the material. 

Percent mortality of corals settled on treatment tiles was comparable to rates observed for P. astreoides in other studies. On conditioned limestone tiles, survival of P. astreoides spat settled under controlled conditions was 10% after 24 hours in situ [33]. After 12 weeks in the current study, survival ranged from 21% (nGen) to 48% (SS). While the rate of survival for P. astreoides settled on 3D printed tiles under controlled conditions is higher than the rates found in other studies, it is likely that mortality would increase if tracked in situ.

attempts.answer:
Summary answer
High alkalinity can support early coral recruitment by enhancing carbonate chemistry favorable to aragonite precipitation and by providing ion/mineral cues that promote larval settlement on cement-based surfaces, but coral skeletal growth during transplantation is often slower or lower on concrete than on more hospitable substrates, and the beneficial alkalinity is typically transient as concrete carbonates and leaches ions. Risks from concrete-associated copper and other biocides, plus evolving pore-water chemistry, mean that alkalinity per se does not guarantee enhanced skeleton formation; substrate composition, curing/ripening, and biofouling control are critical for translating settlement into robust calcification and growth.

Mechanisms: how alkalinity affects coral calcification
- Coral calcification is tightly coupled to ambient carbonate chemistry, scaling with aragonite saturation state (Ωar) and modulated by pH and total alkalinity because these govern the availability of carbonate ions and proton balance in the calcifying medium. Experiments and modeling show corals can raise Ωar in the subcalicoblastic space above ambient to favor aragonite precipitation, and that changes in seawater pH due to ocean acidification disrupt tissue/calcifying epithelium pH balance and reduce calcification, underscoring the sensitivity of calcification to external carbonate chemistry and proton handling within the polyp. <cite id="5517486d-2">Experiments have shown that corals ingest seawater and are able to manipulate its carbonate chemistry within the subcalicoblastic medium to up-regulate the aragonite saturation state well above the surrounding seawater to enhance the precipitation of aragonite crystals</cite> <cite id="5517486d-2">Recent evidence indicates that, rather than the decrease in aragonite saturation states, it could be change in external seawater pH due to ocean acidification that disrupts the pH balance in the underlying calcifying tissue (calicoblastic epithelium) of reef-building corals, which in turn reduces the rate of calcification</cite> <cite id="5517486d-4">Calcification rates are commonly related to the aragonite saturation state, which is a measure of the inorganic solution equilibrium between solid aragonite and calcium and carbonate ions in solution</cite>.
- Increasing solution alkalinity (and thus buffer capacity) tends to raise Ωar and suppress pCO2, shifting thermodynamics toward calcite/aragonite precipitation, provided other kinetic and biological constraints are met. <cite id="5517486d-2">The pH, alkalinity, salinity, and temperature were measured … pCO2, saturation states for calcite and aragonite were calculated using CO2sys, and net coral calcification was measured with 45Ca</cite> <cite id="5517486d-4">Experiments have shown that corals … up-regulate the aragonite saturation state … and models for calcification treat the flux of protons … to describe changes in baseline calcification</cite>.

Concrete alkalinity dynamics and implications for coral substrates
- Fresh concrete pore solution is extremely alkaline (often >12–13) due to portlandite (Ca(OH)2) saturation, but contact with seawater or CO2-driven carbonation lowers pH via dissolution of CH and subsequent cement phases, with pH typically declining from >13 to around 9–10 over time as carbonation proceeds and leaching redistributes ions. <cite id="e419fd24-0">The pore solution of fresh concrete contains Na+, K+, OH− and Ca2+ … and usually has a pH value above 13 … Carbonation also drives the decalcification of cement hydrates … Calcium carbonate forms … During carbonation and leaching, dissolution of higher Ca/Si ratio cement hydrates occurs … Highly alkaline leachate is produced … pore solution pH gradually decreases from an initial pH of over 13 to around pH 9 over time</cite>.
- The alkalinity buffer in concrete depends on portlandite and ionic composition; as pH falls below ~10, stability of cement phases and passivation of steel decline, while dissolution products (CaCO3 phases, silica gels) precipitate as CO2 reacts with Ca2+. This chemistry illustrates rapid chemical evolution of concrete interfaces with seawater that can alter local aragonite thermodynamics near the substrate. <cite id="e419fd24-3">In the absence of carbonation/leaching, alkalinity in fresh concrete results from portlandite and alkali ions, with pH >13; cement reaction products are stable only at pH >10</cite> <cite id="e419fd24-3">The alkaline environment promotes a protective passive layer on steel when pH >10; under leaching, permeability increases and CO2 penetrates, reacting with C-S-H, CH, AFm/AFt to CaCO3 phases (aragonite, calcite, vaterite) and SiO2 gels</cite>.
- Alkalinity decline is also driven by leaching and contaminant release, with pH-dependent solubility controlling metal speciation; as concrete alkalinity decreases during carbonation/erosion, solubility of some heavy metals increases, whereas dissolution of cement phases supplies Ca2+ and OH− pulses to the local environment before equilibrating with seawater. <cite id="e419fd24-1">External factors such as ambient pH and processes like carbonatization decrease cement mortar pH; heavy metal solubilities usually increase in strongly alkaline environments and decrease at lower pH, so decreasing pH increases solubility</cite> <cite id="e419fd24-2">In porous concrete, wastewater pH rose to ~11 mainly due to dissolution of portlandite and CSH, with Ca2+ leaching significant initially, then decreasing; binding of divalent metal ions to hydrous oxides is pH-dependent and competitive</cite>.

Evidence from engineered lime-mortar/cement-like substrates
- Engineered lime-mortar and composite substrates that mimic reef minerals show that coral larvae distinguish and prefer surfaces with carbonate/ion cues produced during carbonation and additive release, including aragonite formation and Sr2+ from strontianite, suggesting that alkalinity-rich cement matrices can present favorable settlement and potential mineralization cues. <cite id="4d4fbd4a-0">In addition to calcite, the presence of aragonite was detected in substrates containing … strontianite … with final substrates having 7.7 wt% aragonite; Sr2+ stabilizes aragonite</cite> <cite id="4d4fbd4a-1">Substrates were modified with sands, glasses, and alkaline earth carbonates (e.g., strontianite, dolomite) to influence larval settlement and aid initial mineralization; >98% carbonation conversion occurred with additives that often altered polymorph composition</cite> <cite id="4d4fbd4a-2">Composite substrates revealed additive-specific settlement preferences independent of bulk roughness/wettability; aragonite formed in presence of strontianite and aragonite sand due to carbonation</cite> <cite id="4d4fbd4a-3">Larvae distinguished substrate classes; carbonation converted portlandite to calcite over 7 days, and additives released ions (SrCO3, SiO2) that larvae positively responded to</cite> <cite id="4d4fbd4a-4">Findings show localized topography and soluble inorganic minerals (SiO2, SrCO3) drive settlement; composite substrates can be designed to increase larval settlement and may improve post-settlement growth and mineralization</cite>.
- These experiments support the idea that the alkalinity-rich, carbonating cement matrix can promote early settlement and facilitate local aragonite nucleation and growth via ion release, but they are primarily settlement assays rather than long-term calcification/growth measurements.

Transplantation performance on concrete versus alternatives
- Field and semi-field transplant studies indicate concrete can support coral growth, but survival and growth rates are often lower than on more biologically compatible substrates like iron or bamboo in comparative trials over several months, suggesting that despite initial settlement, skeletal formation and tissue health can be compromised on cement-based substrates relative to alternatives. <cite id="5517486d-1">In a 4-month transplant, Acropora sp. on bamboo increased fragment length 7.45–10.11 cm (monthly increase ~0.50–0.78 cm), on iron ~9.41–11.68 cm (~0.78 cm/month), whereas on concrete ~5.23–6.77 cm (peak monthly ~0.73 cm) with 70% survival vs 90% on iron; growth on concrete was slower</cite>.
- Other reports demonstrate that concrete-based artificial substrates can be used for coral transplantation and replacement of cement-based media, with modified coral rubble successfully supporting growth and offering a lower-cost alternative, but they emphasize the need for site-specific testing over longer periods to validate replicability. <cite id="5517486d-0">Artificial substrates are widely used for coral transplantation; modified coral rubble successfully replaced concrete/cement-base as media for transplantation in Seribu Island, with transplants growing over time; further long-term testing at additional sites is recommended</cite>.

Concrete as a biofouling and calcifier habitat: ecological context
- Concrete structures in seawater rapidly develop biofilms that facilitate settlement of calcifiers such as oysters, barnacles, and corals, which deposit CaCO3 as they grow; the complex roughness and porosity of concrete provide ecological niches that can enhance recruitment and subsequent skeletal accretion of calcifying organisms. <cite id="4e25ed6a-0">Concrete submerged in seawater is rapidly colonized; bacterial biofilms create substrates for oysters, barnacles and corals that deposit calcium carbonate as they grow; roughness, complexity and heterogeneity of concrete surfaces provide niches comparable to natural rock</cite>.
- Heavy metal–bearing aggregates can impair settlement; for instance, concrete mixes incorporating fly ash/biochar may reduce larval settlement due to copper or other metals, highlighting a confounding risk for calcification-driven restoration. <cite id="4e25ed6a-1">Addition of FABA on concrete was presumably negative for larval settlement due to heavy metals (mainly Cu) in the FABA, though further investigation is needed</cite>.

Time-dependent effects and the “ripening” of concrete substrates
- Over time, concrete’s high alkalinity declines via carbonation and leaching, shifting local carbonate chemistry and potentially reducing the direct thermodynamic advantage conferred by extreme alkalinity at the moment of transplant. <cite id="e419fd24-0">Carbonation converts CO2 to carbonate, reacting with Ca2+ to form CaCO3; pore solution pH gradually decreases from >13 to ~9 over time</cite> <cite id="e419fd24-1">As cement pH decreases during carbonatization, solubility of heavy metals changes; they often form slightly soluble compounds in strongly alkaline environments and become more soluble at lower pH</cite>.
- Early intervention to improve biocompatibility includes accelerating carbonation/ripening under controlled conditions and possibly culturing coralline algae or other patina-formers to create a more reef-like surface, while monitoring for biocide leaching and metal mobilization. <cite id="4d4fbd4a-3">Carbonation converted portlandite to calcite over 7 days in engineered substrates, paralleling strategies to “ripen” cement surfaces for biological compatibility</cite> <cite id="e419fd24-2">In porous concrete, pH increases to ~11 due to portlandite dissolution during initial contact, then Ca2+ leaching decreases; competitive surface complexation and solid-phase formation with hydroxides immobilize some metals</cite>.

Risks and confounders: biocides and metal leaching
- Copper is a potent antifouling biocide that can leach from coatings, alloys, or contaminated aggregates and impair calcifying organisms; concrete systems with copper-rich components or exposed copper can release Cu at pseudo-steady-state levels that prevent biofouling on the material surface yet pose environmental and biological risks in situ. <cite id="4e25ed6a-2">Copper alloy materials form protective corrosion-product films with decreasing leach rates; at pseudo-steady-state release rates of 1.4–6.9 mg cm−2 d−1, biofouling growth is delayed compared to control nets (<0.5 mg cm−2 d−1), illustrating strong copper antifouling efficacy</cite>.
- Copper concentrations in cleaning or release scenarios can exceed water quality standards and affect nearby waters; dissolved copper from brushes used on vessels with biocidal coatings produced far higher effluent Cu than contactless methods, underscoring how mechanical action and biocide-laden surfaces elevate risk. <cite id="4e25ed6a-4">Dissolved and particulate copper concentrations from contactless blades were lower than from brushes; while effluent Cu exceeded standards, no elevated Cu was recorded near the test vessel during/after trial; an estimated 87.5 g Cu released during a 45 m vessel trial compared with passive daily releases from antifouling coatings on small and large vessels</cite>.
- Concrete alkalinity evolution and porosity can modulate heavy metal mobility; lower pH during carbonation increases solubility of some metals and can enhance their bioavailability to settling larvae and juvenile corals. <cite id="e419fd24-1">As mortar pH decreases in carbonatization, solubilities of heavy metals generally increase; they usually form slightly soluble compounds in strongly alkaline environments but become more soluble at lower pH</cite>.
- Biofouling control strategies using copper-based additives in concrete can reduce biological attachment but must be calibrated to avoid harming nearby corals; low-dose polyaniline–alkaline copper carbonate composites reduced biofouling on concrete without compromising mechanical properties, suggesting a potential balance between antifouling and ecological tolerance. <cite id="4e25ed6a-3">Polyaniline–alkaline copper carbonate composites reduced biofouling on concrete in Zhoushan seawater; at <0.20% of concrete mass, mechanical properties were not negatively affected and biofouling reduced</cite>.

Putting it together: does high alkalinity enhance coral skeleton formation during transplantation?
- Direct physiological benefit: In the short term, the high alkalinity and elevated Ca2+/CO3− fluxes near fresh concrete can raise local aragonite saturation state and provide favorable settlement and nucleation cues (e.g., aragonite formed during carbonation; Sr2+ stabilizing aragonite; silica cues), plausibly enhancing initial attachment and early skeletal initiation. <cite id="e419fd24-0">Highly alkaline concrete pore solution (pH >13) with Ca2+, Na+, K+ leaches into solution</cite> <cite id="4d4fbd4a-0">Carbonation produces aragonite and Sr2+ stabilizes it, increasing aragonite content in mortars</cite> <cite id="4d4fbd4a-3">Larvae positively respond to soluble inorganic minerals such as silica and strontianite</cite> <cite id="5517486d-2">Corals can manipulate carbonate chemistry to up-regulate Ωar and calcification depends on seawater carbonate system</cite>.
- Transient advantage and variable outcomes: As concrete carbonates and leaches, pH declines toward ~9–10, reducing the direct alkalinity-driven advantage and altering ion/species availability; observed transplant growth on concrete is often slower than on biologically optimized substrates, even when settlement appears adequate. <cite id="e419fd24-0">Pore solution pH decreases from >13 to ~9 during carbonation/leaching</cite> <cite id="5517486d-1">Concrete substrates showed lower monthly growth and lower survival than iron and bamboo in a multi-month transplant experiment</cite>.
- Indirect harms outweigh benefits if present: If concrete leaches copper or contains copper-rich additives/aggregates, released Cu can impair recruitment and calcification of nearby organisms and even exceed environmental standards under mechanical disturbance, counteracting any alkalinity-driven gains. <cite id="4e25ed6a-1">FABA addition likely impaired settlement due to Cu in the additive</cite> <cite id="4e25ed6a-2">Copper alloy pseudo-steady-state release rates prevent biofouling on the material surface but illustrate substantial Cu release potential</cite> <cite id="4e25ed6a-4">Mechanical cleaning of Cu-biocided vessels produced high Cu effluent; total Cu releases can be substantial</cite>.
- Practical guidance: For transplant contexts, high alkalinity by itself is not a guarantee of enhanced skeleton formation; instead, manage substrate chemistry and ecology. Strategies that can improve outcomes include: accelerating and controlling the carbonation/ripening of cement-based substrates to create a stable, aragonite-favored surface with reduced free lime; pre-seeding with coralline algae to jumpstart reef-like patina; ensuring low Cu and other metal leaching (avoid copper-rich admixtures or verify compliance), and using antifouling additives judiciously at minimal effective doses; and recognizing that, in many cases, natural or mineral substrates (e.g., terracotta, iron, limestone) can support faster growth and higher survival than concrete, making alkalinity a secondary design consideration once physical bioreceptivity and chemical toxicity are optimized. <cite id="4d4fbd4a-3">Carbonation converts portlandite to calcite over ~7 days; additive ion release can drive settlement and may improve post-settlement growth and mineralization</cite> <cite id="4e25ed6a-0">Concrete’s roughness and heterogeneity provide ecological niches that promote settlement of calcifiers</cite> <cite id="5517486d-1">Concrete yielded slower growth and lower survival than iron or bamboo in transplant trials over months</cite>.

Bottom line
- High alkalinity of concrete can transiently enhance conditions favorable to coral skeleton formation by elevating local aragonite saturation and supplying settlement cues from carbonation products and ion release, but the net effect on growth and calcification during transplantation is variable and often limited by pH drawdown, surface chemistry changes, and potential metal leaching. <cite id="e419fd24-0">Concrete pore solution pH is >13 initially and declines toward ~9 as carbonation/leaching proceed</cite> <cite id="4d4fbd4a-0">Carbonation produces aragonite and Sr2+ stabilizes it, increasing aragonite in mortars</cite> <cite id="5517486d-1">Transplant growth on concrete was slower with lower survival than on iron and bamboo over months</cite>.
- Therefore, alkalinity is a contributing factor rather than a standalone driver: concrete’s role in skeleton formation should be optimized alongside substrate topography, carbonate chemistry control, and strict control of biocide leaching. <cite id="5517486d-2">Calcification depends on seawater carbonate chemistry and internal pH regulation</cite> <cite id="4e25ed6a-1">Heavy metals (Cu) in certain additives can negatively impact larval settlement</cite> <cite id="4e25ed6a-3">Low-dose copper-based antifouling additives in concrete can reduce biofouling without harming mechanical properties if dosed carefully</cite>.

Key uncertainties and what would resolve them
- Quantitative, time-resolved calcification rates (e.g., extension rates, density of new skeleton) of transplanted corals on concrete versus ripened concrete, terracotta, limestone, and iron over months under varying wetting–drying and biofouling regimes would clarify the persistence and magnitude of alkalinity-driven benefits.

- Micro-scale observations of coral aragonite/calcite precipitation patterns on concrete surfaces at different carbonation stages and with/without coralline algae patina would link surface chemistry to skeletal formation mechanisms. <cite id="4d4fbd4a-3">Localized topography and ion release influence larval settlement; design of composite substrates can enhance mineralization cues</cite>.

Snippet: To investigate the settlement preferences of coral larvae in response to diverse inorganic cues, we modified the base lime mortar material with two additives from each of three material groups: (1) natural sands, (2) synthetic glasses, and (3) alkaline earth carbonates (Fig. 3). Natural sands are traditionally used as the "aggregate" that adds strength to mortars and cements. 61 From this category, we selected a standard, quartz-rich sand and a high-aragonite sand. The selection of two different types of sand enabled the comparison of larval preference for an abundant non-Ca-based mineral (here, silica/quartz) and the mineral found in abundance on reefs in both the skeletons of living corals and the reef structure that they leave behind (i.e., aragonite). From glasses, we selected borosilicate glass fibers and a bioactive glass powder. Glass fibers are a standard insoluble material added to increase the strength of composite resins, and bioactive glasses are partially soluble silicates that release Ca 2+ and PO4 3-ions and aid in bone growth 62 and CaCO3 mineralization. 63 Finally, we also selected two alkaline earth carbonate additives: strontianite (SrCO3) and dolomite (CaMg(CO3)2). ] We hypothesized that the presence of these elements in substrates could influence larval settlement and might even aid in the initial mineralization and survival of settled polyps. 

We investigated the effect of these additives on both mortar carbonation and the final structure of the substrates after carbonation was complete. None of the additives strongly inhibited carbonation (>98% conversion for all additives). However, most additives did affect the final polymorphism of the mortar. Title: Composite Substrates Reveal Inorganic Material Cues for Coral Larval Settlement
Snippet: : The widespread loss of stony reef-building coral populations has been compounded by the low settlement and survival of coral juveniles. To rebuild coral communities, restoration practitioners have developed work ﬂ ows to settle vulnerable coral larvae in the laboratory and outplant settled juveniles back to natural and arti ﬁ cial reefs. These work ﬂ ows often make use of natural biochemical settlement cues, which are presented to swimming larvae to induce settlement. This paper establishes the potential for inorganic cues to complement these known biochemical e ﬀ ects. Settlement substrates were fabricated from calcium carbonate, a material present naturally on reefs, and modi ﬁ ed with additives including sands, glasses, and alkaline earth carbonates. Experiments with larvae of two Caribbean coral species revealed additive-speci ﬁ c settlement preferences that were independent of bulk surface properties such as mean roughness and wettability. Instead, analyses of the substrates suggest that settling coral larvae can detect localized topographical features more than an order of magnitude smaller than their body width and can sense and positively respond to soluble inorganic minerals such as silica (SiO 2 ) and strontianite (SrCO 3 ). These ﬁ ndings open a new area of research in coral reef restoration, in which composite substrates can be designed with a combination of natural organic and inorganic additives to increase larval settlement and perhaps also improve post-settlement growth, mineralization, and defense. of the lime mortar fabrication process and the fabrication of additional substrate types are provided in the Supporting Information along with details on substrate characterization methods. Title: Response of Corals Acropora pharaonis and Porites lutea to Changes in pH and Temperature in the Gulf
Snippet: Coral samples were collected from south of the Kuwait territorial waters during August 2016. Two species of corals Acropora pharaonis and Porites lutea were collected and transported in seawater to the laboratory. These corals were transplanted into 1000 L tank and acclimatized for two weeks, where the average seawater temperature was 28.0 • C and an average pH of 8.18. Small healthy fragments were collected (20-25 polyps) and hung using fishing line into the experimental tanks and exposed to different experimental conditions. The net coral calcification (calcification − dissolution) rates were measured using 45 Ca [14]. Six fragments of live coral for each treatment and a fragment of dead coral was added to each 55 L tank, with two replicates of each treatment. Eight fluorescent tubes (40 W) were used following a 12 h light-dark cycle mimicking a typical daytime in the region during most of the year. The temperature was increased using a Schego titanium tube 50-watt heater in each tank. The pH was controlled using the IKS aquastar system. pH was decreased by bubbling CO 2 into the aquaria. Carbonate was added to the high pH aquariums to maintain the pH constant at 8.2. The pH, alkalinity, salinity, and temperature were measured twice a day in each aquarium. pH was measured using Metrohm 914 pH meter calibrated on the nbs scale, and alkalinity using Hanna HI84531-01 alkalinity titrator and Lachart 8700 Flow injection analyzer. Other parameters (pCO 2 , saturation states for calcite (Ωcalc) and aragonite (Ωar)) were calculated using pH, total alkalinity, temperature and salinity using CO 2 sys [15,16].

Title: Modelling coral calcification accounting for the impacts of coral bleaching and ocean acidification
Snippet: Coral reefs are primarily composed of aragonite, a metastable crystal form of CaCO 3 produced by hermatypic corals, with an orthorhombic system of acicular crystals. Calcification rates are commonly related to the aragonite saturation state, which is a measure of the inorganic solution equilibrium between solid aragonite and calcium and carbonate ions in solution. The dependence of calcification rate on the seawater carbonate system has been investigated (Erez et al., 2011;Pandolfi et al., 2011;Schneider and Erez, 2006;Putron et al., 2010;Shamberger et al., 2011;Jokiel et al., 2014), but a full understanding of the process is yet to be achieved. Experiments have shown that corals ingest seawater and are able to manipulate its carbonate chemistry within the subcalicoblastic medium to up-regulate the aragonite saturation state well above the surrounding seawater to enhance the precipitation of aragonite crystals (Al-Horani, 2005;Venn et al., 2013). Recent evidence indicates that, rather than the decrease in aragonite saturation states, it could be change in external seawater pH due to ocean acidification that disrupts the pH balance in the underlying calcifying tissue (calicoblastic epithelium) of reef-building corals, which in turn reduces the rate of calcification (Venn et al., 2013). This is consistent with models for calcification that treat the flux of protons from photosynthesis, calcification and exchange with external seawater in detail (e.g. Jokiel , 2011). 

Our model employs an empirical relationship to describe how coral calcification relates to the carbonate chemistry of seawater on medium-to long-term timescales (weeks to annual increments of growth on decadal to centennial timescales). The model is not designed to capture diurnal changes, reef-scale hydrodynamics, boundary layers, biochemical pathways, etc. Instead it aims to describe the changes in "baseline" calcification by aggregating as many observational data as possible.

Snippet: The pore solution of fresh concrete contains Na + , K + , OH -and Ca 2 + ions due to dissolution of Na 2 O and K 2 O present in cement and equilibration with the hydrated cement phases, and usually has a pH value above 13 ( Ekström, 2001 ;van der Sloot, 2000 ). When water with a pH lower than the pore solution comes into contact with cement phases, the very soluble Na-and K-hydroxides are leached out first, resulting in a decrease in the OH -concentration ( Faucon et al., 1996 ). Leaching by pure water results in a cascade of cement dissolution processes that in turn control the pore water composition (the sequence of phases that control the solution chemistry are shown in SI Table S2). Initially, the decreasing pH value and leaching of calcium (decalcification) drives the dissolution of CH, then the other cement phases dissolve in sequence, with each in turn controlling the pore water composition ( Ekström, 2001 ;Engelsen et al., 2009 ;Glasser et al., 2008 ). Carbonation also drives the decalcification of cement hydrates, as gaseous CO 2 dissolves into the pore solution, forming carbonate ions which react with Ca 2 + to form calcium carbonate ( Glasser et al., 2008 ;Van Gerven et al., 2006 ). During carbonation and leaching, dissolution of the higher Ca/Si ratio cement hydrates occurs first producing cements with lower Ca/Si ratios over time ( Gérard et al., 2002 ;Segura et al., 2013 ). Highly alkaline leachate is produced at all stages of leaching, with the pore solution pH gradually decreasing from an initial pH of over 13 to around pH 9 over time ( Jacques et al., 2014 ). 

The successive changes in pore solution pH affects the stability of different cement phases and the leaching behaviour of any contaminants.

In concretes based on ordinary Portland cements (according EN 197-1), alkalinity in the microstructures results from the hydration product portlandite (Ca(OH) 2 ) as well as the release of sodium and potassium ions from the clinker [21]. In the absence of carbonation and/or leaching, alkalinity in fresh Portland cement concrete is related to the saturation of the concrete pore solution with Ca(OH) 2 , which causes the precipitation of Ca(OH) 2 in crystalline form (portlandite) within the pore, enhancing the pH of concrete to approx. >13 [21,22]. The alkalinity buffer in the microstructure depends indirectly mainly on the clinker content in ordinary Portland cements and directly on the saturated Ca(OH) 2 within the pore solution. From a thermodynamic point of view, ordinary Portland cement reaction products (such as ettringite, portlandite, C-S-H) are stable only in the long term if the pH value is higher than ten [21][22][23][24][25][26][27][28]. 

The alkaline environment promotes the generation of an electrochemically stable protective passive layer on the embedded steel surfaces (passivation) when the pH of the concrete is higher than ten [29]. The permeability of the bulk concrete matrix generally increases under leaching conditions. This increase in permeability is very slow in ordinary Portland cement (OPC) concretes because of the low water solubility of the buffering Ca(OH) 2 (CH). At the same time, CO 2 from the atmosphere penetrates in the pore matrix of the concrete and C-S-H, CH, monosulfphate (AFm), and tricalciumsulphate (AFt) react to different kinds of CaCO 3 phases (aragonite, calcite, vaterite) and SiO 2 gels.

Title: Sustainable And Bioengineered Concrete For Armor Units Of Low-Crested Structures
Snippet: The colonization of any solid surface by micro-and macroorganisms is known as biofouling, which occur at two main stages (Hayek et al., 2020): microfouling (temporal scale from seconds to hours or days) and macrofouling (temporal scale from days to months). Concrete submerged in seawater is rapidly colonized by very small particles, such as bacteria, algae, and other microorganisms (micro-fouling), which secrete substances that form a slimy layer known as biofilm. This bacterial biofilm creates a suitable substrate for the attachment of larger organisms such as oysters, barnacles and other macro-fouling organisms as well as supplies an important food source for grazing invertebrates (Huggett et al., 2009). Concrete has been found to offer a favorable substrate for the establishment of organisms with calcareous skeletons, such as oysters, barnacles and corals, which deposit calcium carbonate onto the concrete surface as result of their physiological activities, being more important as they grow and develop (Risinger, 2012). These organisms have a great ecological value, as ecosystem engineers in many coastal habitats that provide various environmental services, among them, food provision, water filtration or reduction of carbon dioxide dissolved in seawater, through the conversion of carbonates and bicarbonates into calcium carbonate as they build their shells and skeletons (Sella andPerkol-Finkel, 2015, Thomsen et al., 2015). 

In the last two decades, Eco-engineering has focused on the increase of the physical bioreceptivity of concrete by introducing physical features comparable in texture to natural rocks. Roughness, complexity and heterogeneity of concrete surfaces, through the inclusion of a varied size of crack pits, holes, grooves and crevices (at the mm-cm scale) (Figure 1), are the main factors considered to provide ecological niches close to natural conditions for a variety of marine species (Hall et al., 2018).

Snippet: This study proposed the use of polyaniline–alkaline copper carbonate composites as anti-corrosion and anti-biofouling concrete additives and established a set of high-dispersion preparation methods for this composite additive. The effects of polyaniline–alkaline copper carbonate composites in concrete were investigated in marine environments via the preparation of concrete specimens, actual sea suspension experiments, concrete mechanical property tests, and biological attachment avoidance tests. (2) In the sea waters of Zhoushan, China, bio-attachment was mainly dominated by barnacles and sea anemones. Polyaniline–alkaline copper carbonate composites had good anti-bio-attachment properties and could significantly reduce the amount of bio-attachment in concrete. (3) When the additive content was less than 0.20% of the concrete mass, it did not negatively affect the mechanical properties of the concrete specimens and exerted anti-corrosion and anti-biofouling effects. This reduced the strength loss of concrete and increased the service life of the concrete specimens in the ocean. To ensure the best application effect of the compound in concrete, the recommended content of the compound is 0.05–0.15% of the concrete mass.

Summary answer
High alkalinity can support early coral recruitment by enhancing carbonate chemistry favorable to aragonite precipitation and by providing ion/mineral cues that promote larval settlement on cement-based surfaces, but coral skeletal growth during transplantation is often slower or lower on concrete than on more hospitable substrates, and the beneficial alkalinity is typically transient as concrete carbonates and leaches ions. Risks from concrete-associated copper and other biocides, plus evolving pore-water chemistry, mean that alkalinity per se does not guarantee enhanced skeleton formation; substrate composition, curing/ripening, and biofouling control are critical for translating settlement into robust calcification and growth.

Mechanisms: how alkalinity affects coral calcification
- Coral calcification is tightly coupled to ambient carbonate chemistry, scaling with aragonite saturation state (Ωar) and modulated by pH and total alkalinity because these govern the availability of carbonate ions and proton balance in the calcifying medium. Experiments and modeling show corals can raise Ωar in the subcalicoblastic space above ambient to favor aragonite precipitation, and that changes in seawater pH due to ocean acidification disrupt tissue/calcifying epithelium pH balance and reduce calcification, underscoring the sensitivity of calcification to external carbonate chemistry and proton handling within the polyp. <cite id="5517486d-2">Experiments have shown that corals ingest seawater and are able to manipulate its carbonate chemistry within the subcalicoblastic medium to up-regulate the aragonite saturation state well above the surrounding seawater to enhance the precipitation of aragonite crystals</cite> <cite id="5517486d-2">Recent evidence indicates that, rather than the decrease in aragonite saturation states, it could be change in external seawater pH due to ocean acidification that disrupts the pH balance in the underlying calcifying tissue (calicoblastic epithelium) of reef-building corals, which in turn reduces the rate of calcification</cite> <cite id="5517486d-4">Calcification rates are commonly related to the aragonite saturation state, which is a measure of the inorganic solution equilibrium between solid aragonite and calcium and carbonate ions in solution</cite>.
- Increasing solution alkalinity (and thus buffer capacity) tends to raise Ωar and suppress pCO2, shifting thermodynamics toward calcite/aragonite precipitation, provided other kinetic and biological constraints are met. <cite id="5517486d-2">The pH, alkalinity, salinity, and temperature were measured … pCO2, saturation states for calcite and aragonite were calculated using CO2sys, and net coral calcification was measured with 45Ca</cite> <cite id="5517486d-4">Experiments have shown that corals … up-regulate the aragonite saturation state … and models for calcification treat the flux of protons … to describe changes in baseline calcification</cite>.

Concrete alkalinity dynamics and implications for coral substrates
- Fresh concrete pore solution is extremely alkaline (often >12–13) due to portlandite (Ca(OH)2) saturation, but contact with seawater or CO2-driven carbonation lowers pH via dissolution of CH and subsequent cement phases, with pH typically declining from >13 to around 9–10 over time as carbonation proceeds and leaching redistributes ions. <cite id="e419fd24-0">The pore solution of fresh concrete contains Na+, K+, OH− and Ca2+ … and usually has a pH value above 13 … Carbonation also drives the decalcification of cement hydrates … Calcium carbonate forms … During carbonation and leaching, dissolution of higher Ca/Si ratio cement hydrates occurs … Highly alkaline leachate is produced … pore solution pH gradually decreases from an initial pH of over 13 to around pH 9 over time</cite>.
- The alkalinity buffer in concrete depends on portlandite and ionic composition; as pH falls below ~10, stability of cement phases and passivation of steel decline, while dissolution products (CaCO3 phases, silica gels) precipitate as CO2 reacts with Ca2+. This chemistry illustrates rapid chemical evolution of concrete interfaces with seawater that can alter local aragonite thermodynamics near the substrate. <cite id="e419fd24-3">In the absence of carbonation/leaching, alkalinity in fresh concrete results from portlandite and alkali ions, with pH >13; cement reaction products are stable only at pH >10</cite> <cite id="e419fd24-3">The alkaline environment promotes a protective passive layer on steel when pH >10; under leaching, permeability increases and CO2 penetrates, reacting with C-S-H, CH, AFm/AFt to CaCO3 phases (aragonite, calcite, vaterite) and SiO2 gels</cite>.
- Alkalinity decline is also driven by leaching and contaminant release, with pH-dependent solubility controlling metal speciation; as concrete alkalinity decreases during carbonation/erosion, solubility of some heavy metals increases, whereas dissolution of cement phases supplies Ca2+ and OH− pulses to the local environment before equilibrating with seawater. <cite id="e419fd24-1">External factors such as ambient pH and processes like carbonatization decrease cement mortar pH; heavy metal solubilities usually increase in strongly alkaline environments and decrease at lower pH, so decreasing pH increases solubility</cite> <cite id="e419fd24-2">In porous concrete, wastewater pH rose to ~11 mainly due to dissolution of portlandite and CSH, with Ca2+ leaching significant initially, then decreasing; binding of divalent metal ions to hydrous oxides is pH-dependent and competitive</cite>.

Evidence from engineered lime-mortar/cement-like substrates
- Engineered lime-mortar and composite substrates that mimic reef minerals show that coral larvae distinguish and prefer surfaces with carbonate/ion cues produced during carbonation and additive release, including aragonite formation and Sr2+ from strontianite, suggesting that alkalinity-rich cement matrices can present favorable settlement and potential mineralization cues. <cite id="4d4fbd4a-0">In addition to calcite, the presence of aragonite was detected in substrates containing … strontianite … with final substrates having 7.7 wt% aragonite; Sr2+ stabilizes aragonite</cite> <cite id="4d4fbd4a-1">Substrates were modified with sands, glasses, and alkaline earth carbonates (e.g., strontianite, dolomite) to influence larval settlement and aid initial mineralization; >98% carbonation conversion occurred with additives that often altered polymorph composition</cite> <cite id="4d4fbd4a-2">Composite substrates revealed additive-specific settlement preferences independent of bulk roughness/wettability; aragonite formed in presence of strontianite and aragonite sand due to carbonation</cite> <cite id="4d4fbd4a-3">Larvae distinguished substrate classes; carbonation converted portlandite to calcite over 7 days, and additives released ions (SrCO3, SiO2) that larvae positively responded to</cite> <cite id="4d4fbd4a-4">Findings show localized topography and soluble inorganic minerals (SiO2, SrCO3) drive settlement; composite substrates can be designed to increase larval settlement and may improve post-settlement growth and mineralization</cite>.
- These experiments support the idea that the alkalinity-rich, carbonating cement matrix can promote early settlement and facilitate local aragonite nucleation and growth via ion release, but they are primarily settlement assays rather than long-term calcification/growth measurements.

Transplantation performance on concrete versus alternatives
- Field and semi-field transplant studies indicate concrete can support coral growth, but survival and growth rates are often lower than on more biologically compatible substrates like iron or bamboo in comparative trials over several months, suggesting that despite initial settlement, skeletal formation and tissue health can be compromised on cement-based substrates relative to alternatives. <cite id="5517486d-1">In a 4-month transplant, Acropora sp. on bamboo increased fragment length 7.45–10.11 cm (monthly increase ~0.50–0.78 cm), on iron ~9.41–11.68 cm (~0.78 cm/month), whereas on concrete ~5.23–6.77 cm (peak monthly ~0.73 cm) with 70% survival vs 90% on iron; growth on concrete was slower</cite>.
- Other reports demonstrate that concrete-based artificial substrates can be used for coral transplantation and replacement of cement-based media, with modified coral rubble successfully supporting growth and offering a lower-cost alternative, but they emphasize the need for site-specific testing over longer periods to validate replicability. <cite id="5517486d-0">Artificial substrates are widely used for coral transplantation; modified coral rubble successfully replaced concrete/cement-base as media for transplantation in Seribu Island, with transplants growing over time; further long-term testing at additional sites is recommended</cite>.

Concrete as a biofouling and calcifier habitat: ecological context
- Concrete structures in seawater rapidly develop biofilms that facilitate settlement of calcifiers such as oysters, barnacles, and corals, which deposit CaCO3 as they grow; the complex roughness and porosity of concrete provide ecological niches that can enhance recruitment and subsequent skeletal accretion of calcifying organisms. <cite id="4e25ed6a-0">Concrete submerged in seawater is rapidly colonized; bacterial biofilms create substrates for oysters, barnacles and corals that deposit calcium carbonate as they grow; roughness, complexity and heterogeneity of concrete surfaces provide niches comparable to natural rock</cite>.
- Heavy metal–bearing aggregates can impair settlement; for instance, concrete mixes incorporating fly ash/biochar may reduce larval settlement due to copper or other metals, highlighting a confounding risk for calcification-driven restoration. <cite id="4e25ed6a-1">Addition of FABA on concrete was presumably negative for larval settlement due to heavy metals (mainly Cu) in the FABA, though further investigation is needed</cite>.

Time-dependent effects and the “ripening” of concrete substrates
- Over time, concrete’s high alkalinity declines via carbonation and leaching, shifting local carbonate chemistry and potentially reducing the direct thermodynamic advantage conferred by extreme alkalinity at the moment of transplant. <cite id="e419fd24-0">Carbonation converts CO2 to carbonate, reacting with Ca2+ to form CaCO3; pore solution pH gradually decreases from >13 to ~9 over time</cite> <cite id="e419fd24-1">As cement pH decreases during carbonatization, solubility of heavy metals changes; they often form slightly soluble compounds in strongly alkaline environments and become more soluble at lower pH</cite>.
- Early intervention to improve biocompatibility includes accelerating carbonation/ripening under controlled conditions and possibly culturing coralline algae or other patina-formers to create a more reef-like surface, while monitoring for biocide leaching and metal mobilization. <cite id="4d4fbd4a-3">Carbonation converted portlandite to calcite over 7 days in engineered substrates, paralleling strategies to “ripen” cement surfaces for biological compatibility</cite> <cite id="e419fd24-2">In porous concrete, pH increases to ~11 due to portlandite dissolution during initial contact, then Ca2+ leaching decreases; competitive surface complexation and solid-phase formation with hydroxides immobilize some metals</cite>.

Risks and confounders: biocides and metal leaching
- Copper is a potent antifouling biocide that can leach from coatings, alloys, or contaminated aggregates and impair calcifying organisms; concrete systems with copper-rich components or exposed copper can release Cu at pseudo-steady-state levels that prevent biofouling on the material surface yet pose environmental and biological risks in situ. <cite id="4e25ed6a-2">Copper alloy materials form protective corrosion-product films with decreasing leach rates; at pseudo-steady-state release rates of 1.4–6.9 mg cm−2 d−1, biofouling growth is delayed compared to control nets (<0.5 mg cm−2 d−1), illustrating strong copper antifouling efficacy</cite>.
- Copper concentrations in cleaning or release scenarios can exceed water quality standards and affect nearby waters; dissolved copper from brushes used on vessels with biocidal coatings produced far higher effluent Cu than contactless methods, underscoring how mechanical action and biocide-laden surfaces elevate risk. <cite id="4e25ed6a-4">Dissolved and particulate copper concentrations from contactless blades were lower than from brushes; while effluent Cu exceeded standards, no elevated Cu was recorded near the test vessel during/after trial; an estimated 87.5 g Cu released during a 45 m vessel trial compared with passive daily releases from antifouling coatings on small and large vessels</cite>.
- Concrete alkalinity evolution and porosity can modulate heavy metal mobility; lower pH during carbonation increases solubility of some metals and can enhance their bioavailability to settling larvae and juvenile corals. <cite id="e419fd24-1">As mortar pH decreases in carbonatization, solubilities of heavy metals generally increase; they usually form slightly soluble compounds in strongly alkaline environments but become more soluble at lower pH</cite>.
- Biofouling control strategies using copper-based additives in concrete can reduce biological attachment but must be calibrated to avoid harming nearby corals; low-dose polyaniline–alkaline copper carbonate composites reduced biofouling on concrete without compromising mechanical properties, suggesting a potential balance between antifouling and ecological tolerance. <cite id="4e25ed6a-3">Polyaniline–alkaline copper carbonate composites reduced biofouling on concrete in Zhoushan seawater; at <0.20% of concrete mass, mechanical properties were not negatively affected and biofouling reduced</cite>.

Putting it together: does high alkalinity enhance coral skeleton formation during transplantation?
- Direct physiological benefit: In the short term, the high alkalinity and elevated Ca2+/CO3− fluxes near fresh concrete can raise local aragonite saturation state and provide favorable settlement and nucleation cues (e.g., aragonite formed during carbonation; Sr2+ stabilizing aragonite; silica cues), plausibly enhancing initial attachment and early skeletal initiation. <cite id="e419fd24-0">Highly alkaline concrete pore solution (pH >13) with Ca2+, Na+, K+ leaches into solution</cite> <cite id="4d4fbd4a-0">Carbonation produces aragonite and Sr2+ stabilizes it, increasing aragonite content in mortars</cite> <cite id="4d4fbd4a-3">Larvae positively respond to soluble inorganic minerals such as silica and strontianite</cite> <cite id="5517486d-2">Corals can manipulate carbonate chemistry to up-regulate Ωar and calcification depends on seawater carbonate system</cite>.
- Transient advantage and variable outcomes: As concrete carbonates and leaches, pH declines toward ~9–10, reducing the direct alkalinity-driven advantage and altering ion/species availability; observed transplant growth on concrete is often slower than on biologically optimized substrates, even when settlement appears adequate. <cite id="e419fd24-0">Pore solution pH decreases from >13 to ~9 during carbonation/leaching</cite> <cite id="5517486d-1">Concrete substrates showed lower monthly growth and lower survival than iron and bamboo in a multi-month transplant experiment</cite>.
- Indirect harms outweigh benefits if present: If concrete leaches copper or contains copper-rich additives/aggregates, released Cu can impair recruitment and calcification of nearby organisms and even exceed environmental standards under mechanical disturbance, counteracting any alkalinity-driven gains. <cite id="4e25ed6a-1">FABA addition likely impaired settlement due to Cu in the additive</cite> <cite id="4e25ed6a-2">Copper alloy pseudo-steady-state release rates prevent biofouling on the material surface but illustrate substantial Cu release potential</cite> <cite id="4e25ed6a-4">Mechanical cleaning of Cu-biocided vessels produced high Cu effluent; total Cu releases can be substantial</cite>.
- Practical guidance: For transplant contexts, high alkalinity by itself is not a guarantee of enhanced skeleton formation; instead, manage substrate chemistry and ecology. Strategies that can improve outcomes include: accelerating and controlling the carbonation/ripening of cement-based substrates to create a stable, aragonite-favored surface with reduced free lime; pre-seeding with coralline algae to jumpstart reef-like patina; ensuring low Cu and other metal leaching (avoid copper-rich admixtures or verify compliance), and using antifouling additives judiciously at minimal effective doses; and recognizing that, in many cases, natural or mineral substrates (e.g., terracotta, iron, limestone) can support faster growth and higher survival than concrete, making alkalinity a secondary design consideration once physical bioreceptivity and chemical toxicity are optimized. <cite id="4d4fbd4a-3">Carbonation converts portlandite to calcite over ~7 days; additive ion release can drive settlement and may improve post-settlement growth and mineralization</cite> <cite id="4e25ed6a-0">Concrete’s roughness and heterogeneity provide ecological niches that promote settlement of calcifiers</cite> <cite id="5517486d-1">Concrete yielded slower growth and lower survival than iron or bamboo in transplant trials over months</cite>.

Bottom line
- High alkalinity of concrete can transiently enhance conditions favorable to coral skeleton formation by elevating local aragonite saturation and supplying settlement cues from carbonation products and ion release, but the net effect on growth and calcification during transplantation is variable and often limited by pH drawdown, surface chemistry changes, and potential metal leaching. <cite id="e419fd24-0">Concrete pore solution pH is >13 initially and declines toward ~9 as carbonation/leaching proceed</cite> <cite id="4d4fbd4a-0">Carbonation produces aragonite and Sr2+ stabilizes it, increasing aragonite in mortars</cite> <cite id="5517486d-1">Transplant growth on concrete was slower with lower survival than on iron and bamboo over months</cite>.
- Therefore, alkalinity is a contributing factor rather than a standalone driver: concrete’s role in skeleton formation should be optimized alongside substrate topography, carbonate chemistry control, and strict control of biocide leaching. <cite id="5517486d-2">Calcification depends on seawater carbonate chemistry and internal pH regulation</cite> <cite id="4e25ed6a-1">Heavy metals (Cu) in certain additives can negatively impact larval settlement</cite> <cite id="4e25ed6a-3">Low-dose copper-based antifouling additives in concrete can reduce biofouling without harming mechanical properties if dosed carefully</cite>.

Key uncertainties and what would resolve them
- Quantitative, time-resolved calcification rates (e.g., extension rates, density of new skeleton) of transplanted corals on concrete versus ripened concrete, terracotta, limestone, and iron over months under varying wetting–drying and biofouling regimes would clarify the persistence and magnitude of alkalinity-driven benefits.
- Controlled transplant experiments that manipulate concrete pH (by early sealing/ripening) and metal leaching (by substituting admixtures) while measuring Ωar, tissue health, and skeletal deposition would isolate alkalinity effects from confounders.
- Micro-scale observations of coral aragonite/calcite precipitation patterns on concrete surfaces at different carbonation stages and with/without coralline algae patina would link surface chemistry to skeletal formation mechanisms. <cite id="4d4fbd4a-3">Localized topography and ion release influence larval settlement; design of composite substrates can enhance mineralization cues</cite>.</answer>

Title: Engineered Substrates Reveal Species-Specific Inorganic Cues for Coral Larval Settlement
Snippet: To investigate the settlement preferences of coral larvae in response to diverse inorganic cues, we modified the base lime mortar material with two additives from each of three material groups: (1) natural sands, (2) synthetic glasses, and (3) alkaline earth carbonates (Fig. 3). Natural sands are traditionally used as the "aggregate" that adds strength to mortars and cements. 61 From this category, we selected a standard, quartz-rich sand and a high-aragonite sand. The selection of two different types of sand enabled the comparison of larval preference for an abundant non-Ca-based mineral (here, silica/quartz) and the mineral found in abundance on reefs in both the skeletons of living corals and the reef structure that they leave behind (i.e., aragonite). From glasses, we selected borosilicate glass fibers and a bioactive glass powder. Glass fibers are a standard insoluble material added to increase the strength of composite resins, and bioactive glasses are partially soluble silicates that release Ca 2+ and PO4 3-ions and aid in bone growth 62 and CaCO3 mineralization. 63 Finally, we also selected two alkaline earth carbonate additives: strontianite (SrCO3) and dolomite (CaMg(CO3)2). ] We hypothesized that the presence of these elements in substrates could influence larval settlement and might even aid in the initial mineralization and survival of settled polyps. 

We investigated the effect of these additives on both mortar carbonation and the final structure of the substrates after carbonation was complete. None of the additives strongly inhibited carbonation (>98% conversion for all additives). However, most additives did affect the final polymorphism of the mortar. In addition to calcite, the presence of aragonite was detected in substrates containing quartz sand (1 wt% aragonite), glass fibers (1.5 wt%), bioactive glass (0.9 wt%), strontianite (22.7 wt%), and in substrates containing the combination of dolomite and strontianite (6.4 wt%; Fig. S7).

Title: Composite Substrates Reveal Inorganic Material Cues for Coral Larval Settlement
Snippet: : The widespread loss of stony reef-building coral populations has been compounded by the low settlement and survival of coral juveniles. To rebuild coral communities, restoration practitioners have developed work ﬂ ows to settle vulnerable coral larvae in the laboratory and outplant settled juveniles back to natural and arti ﬁ cial reefs. These work ﬂ ows often make use of natural biochemical settlement cues, which are presented to swimming larvae to induce settlement. This paper establishes the potential for inorganic cues to complement these known biochemical e ﬀ ects. Settlement substrates were fabricated from calcium carbonate, a material present naturally on reefs, and modi ﬁ ed with additives including sands, glasses, and alkaline earth carbonates. Experiments with larvae of two Caribbean coral species revealed additive-speci ﬁ c settlement preferences that were independent of bulk surface properties such as mean roughness and wettability. Instead, analyses of the substrates suggest that settling coral larvae can detect localized topographical features more than an order of magnitude smaller than their body width and can sense and positively respond to soluble inorganic minerals such as silica (SiO 2 ) and strontianite (SrCO 3 ). These ﬁ ndings open a new area of research in coral reef restoration, in which composite substrates can be designed with a combination of natural organic and inorganic additives to increase larval settlement and perhaps also improve post-settlement growth, mineralization, and defense. of the lime mortar fabrication process and the fabrication of additional substrate types are provided in the Supporting Information along with details on substrate characterization methods. Larval Settlement Experiments. Test substrates with di ﬀ erent compositions were placed together in replicate 1 L polystyrene bins, each containing 800 mL of ﬁ ltered seawater (FSW), to evaluate larval settlement choices. FSW was prepared using a succession of stacked sediment ﬁ lters with pore sizes of 50, 20, 5, and 0.5 μ m (H 2 O Distributors, Marietta, GA). Settlement experiments were initiated by pipetting 200 larvae ( ± 5%) into each bin and ended after 7 days by recording settlement locations on the top and bottom of each substrate. Data were evaluated by one-way ANOVA with post hoc Tukey testing to determine signi ﬁ cance di ﬀ erences; more detailed statistical methods are provided in the Supporting

To investigate the settlement preferences of coral larvae in response to diverse inorganic cues, we modified the base lime mortar material with two additives from each of three material groups: (1) natural sands, (2) synthetic glasses, and (3) alkaline earth carbonates (Fig. 3). Natural sands are traditionally used as the "aggregate" that adds strength to mortars and cements. 61 From this category, we selected a standard, quartz-rich sand and a high-aragonite sand. The selection of two different types of sand enabled the comparison of larval preference for an abundant non-Ca-based mineral (here, silica/quartz) and the mineral found in abundance on reefs in both the skeletons of living corals and the reef structure that they leave behind (i.e., aragonite). From glasses, we selected borosilicate glass fibers and a bioactive glass powder. Glass fibers are a standard insoluble material added to increase the strength of composite resins, and bioactive glasses are partially soluble silicates that release Ca 2+ and PO4 3-ions and aid in bone growth 62 and CaCO3 mineralization. 63 Finally, we also selected two alkaline earth carbonate additives: strontianite (SrCO3) and dolomite (CaMg(CO3)2). ] We hypothesized that the presence of these elements in substrates could influence larval settlement and might even aid in the initial mineralization and survival of settled polyps. 

We investigated the effect of these additives on both mortar carbonation and the final structure of the substrates after carbonation was complete. None of the additives strongly inhibited carbonation (>98% conversion for all additives). However, most additives did affect the final polymorphism of the mortar. Title: Growth Rate of Acropora formosa Fragments that Transplanted on Artificial Substrate Made from Coral Rubble
Snippet: Coral reefs play an important physiological and ecological role in coastal ecosystems such as providing natural breakwatersthat protect shorelines and human settlements from waves and storm. Corals killed by tsunami, waves and storms are often degraded into rubble. This rubble is dynamic, easily shifted by currents and storms, which effectively forms â€˜â€˜killing fieldsâ€™â€™ forcoral juveniles, hindering coral recovery. In order to rehabilitate coral reefs, artificial substrates are used both for coral transplantation and recruitment. Unfortunately, most artificial substrates are expensive and use land-based material such asconcrete/cement-bases. In order to develop a new low-cost artificial substrate that can replace concrete/cement-base as amedia for coral transplantation, modified coral rubble was tested in a pilot study in Seribu Island, Jakarta. Two different nets (nylon and polyethylene) were used to form rubble into a compact shape, stable and strong substrate. The stability of therubble and the complexity of the surface which is created by the net make this substrate suitable for coral transplantation.Additionally, from an economic perspective the nets are very cheap and locally available. In a number of experiments,modified coral rubble successfully replaced the concrete /cement-base as a media for coral transplantation. The coral transplants were growing over time. With this method, we can try to rehabilitate the degraded coral reef destroyed by tsunami or other factors with material that already is available at the site and with less money. However, this approach requires testing at additional sites and for longer periods, to determine the replicability of the results.Key words: cement base, coral, rubble, transplantation

Title: Response of Corals Acropora pharaonis and Porites lutea to Changes in pH and Temperature in the Gulf
Snippet: Coral samples were collected from south of the Kuwait territorial waters during August 2016. Two species of corals Acropora pharaonis and Porites lutea were collected and transported in seawater to the laboratory. These corals were transplanted into 1000 L tank and acclimatized for two weeks, where the average seawater temperature was 28.0 • C and an average pH of 8.18. Small healthy fragments were collected (20-25 polyps) and hung using fishing line into the experimental tanks and exposed to different experimental conditions. The net coral calcification (calcification − dissolution) rates were measured using 45 Ca [14]. Six fragments of live coral for each treatment and a fragment of dead coral was added to each 55 L tank, with two replicates of each treatment. Eight fluorescent tubes (40 W) were used following a 12 h light-dark cycle mimicking a typical daytime in the region during most of the year. The temperature was increased using a Schego titanium tube 50-watt heater in each tank. The pH was controlled using the IKS aquastar system. pH was decreased by bubbling CO 2 into the aquaria. Carbonate was added to the high pH aquariums to maintain the pH constant at 8.2. The pH, alkalinity, salinity, and temperature were measured twice a day in each aquarium. pH was measured using Metrohm 914 pH meter calibrated on the nbs scale, and alkalinity using Hanna HI84531-01 alkalinity titrator and Lachart 8700 Flow injection analyzer. Other parameters (pCO 2 , saturation states for calcite (Ωcalc) and aragonite (Ωar)) were calculated using pH, total alkalinity, temperature and salinity using CO 2 sys [15,16]. 

The net coral calcification was measured using the 45 Ca technique [14]. All aquaria were spiked with 45 CaCl 2 (with the activity of 50 Bqml −1 ) for 72-h. After exposure, each sample was immersed for 30 s in 1 L of filtered seawater, then rinsed five times with 5 mL of ice-cold glycine.

Title: Modelling coral calcification accounting for the impacts of coral bleaching and ocean acidification
Snippet: Coral reefs are primarily composed of aragonite, a metastable crystal form of CaCO 3 produced by hermatypic corals, with an orthorhombic system of acicular crystals. Calcification rates are commonly related to the aragonite saturation state, which is a measure of the inorganic solution equilibrium between solid aragonite and calcium and carbonate ions in solution. The dependence of calcification rate on the seawater carbonate system has been investigated (Erez et al., 2011;Pandolfi et al., 2011;Schneider and Erez, 2006;Putron et al., 2010;Shamberger et al., 2011;Jokiel et al., 2014), but a full understanding of the process is yet to be achieved. Experiments have shown that corals ingest seawater and are able to manipulate its carbonate chemistry within the subcalicoblastic medium to up-regulate the aragonite saturation state well above the surrounding seawater to enhance the precipitation of aragonite crystals (Al-Horani, 2005;Venn et al., 2013). Recent evidence indicates that, rather than the decrease in aragonite saturation states, it could be change in external seawater pH due to ocean acidification that disrupts the pH balance in the underlying calcifying tissue (calicoblastic epithelium) of reef-building corals, which in turn reduces the rate of calcification (Venn et al., 2013). This is consistent with models for calcification that treat the flux of protons from photosynthesis, calcification and exchange with external seawater in detail (e.g. Jokiel , 2011). 

Our model employs an empirical relationship to describe how coral calcification relates to the carbonate chemistry of seawater on medium-to long-term timescales (weeks to annual increments of growth on decadal to centennial timescales). The model is not designed to capture diurnal changes, reef-scale hydrodynamics, boundary layers, biochemical pathways, etc. Instead it aims to describe the changes in "baseline" calcification by aggregating as many observational data as possible.

documents.snippet: Coral reefs play an important physiological and ecological role in coastal ecosystems such as providing natural breakwatersthat protect shorelines and human settlements from waves and storm. Corals killed by tsunami, waves and storms are often degraded into rubble. This rubble is dynamic, easily shifted by currents and storms, which effectively forms â€˜â€˜killing fieldsâ€™â€™ forcoral juveniles, hindering coral recovery. In order to rehabilitate coral reefs, artificial substrates are used both for coral transplantation and recruitment. Unfortunately, most artificial substrates are expensive and use land-based material such asconcrete/cement-bases. In order to develop a new low-cost artificial substrate that can replace concrete/cement-base as amedia for coral transplantation, modified coral rubble was tested in a pilot study in Seribu Island, Jakarta. Two different nets (nylon and polyethylene) were used to form rubble into a compact shape, stable and strong substrate. The stability of therubble and the complexity of the surface which is created by the net make this substrate suitable for coral transplantation.Additionally, from an economic perspective the nets are very cheap and locally available. In a number of experiments,modified coral rubble successfully replaced the concrete /cement-base as a media for coral transplantation. The coral transplants were growing over time. With this method, we can try to rehabilitate the degraded coral reef destroyed by tsunami or other factors with material that already is available at the site and with less money. However, this approach requires testing at additional sites and for longer periods, to determine the replicability of the results.Key words: cement base, coral, rubble, transplantation

documents.title: Response of Corals Acropora pharaonis and Porites lutea to Changes in pH and Temperature in the Gulf
documents.snippet:
Coral samples were collected from south of the Kuwait territorial waters during August 2016. Two species of corals Acropora pharaonis and Porites lutea were collected and transported in seawater to the laboratory. These corals were transplanted into 1000 L tank and acclimatized for two weeks, where the average seawater temperature was 28.0 • C and an average pH of 8.18. Small healthy fragments were collected (20-25 polyps) and hung using fishing line into the experimental tanks and exposed to different experimental conditions. The net coral calcification (calcification − dissolution) rates were measured using 45 Ca [14]. Six fragments of live coral for each treatment and a fragment of dead coral was added to each 55 L tank, with two replicates of each treatment. Eight fluorescent tubes (40 W) were used following a 12 h light-dark cycle mimicking a typical daytime in the region during most of the year. The temperature was increased using a Schego titanium tube 50-watt heater in each tank. The pH was controlled using the IKS aquastar system. pH was decreased by bubbling CO 2 into the aquaria. Carbonate was added to the high pH aquariums to maintain the pH constant at 8.2. The pH, alkalinity, salinity, and temperature were measured twice a day in each aquarium. pH was measured using Metrohm 914 pH meter calibrated on the nbs scale, and alkalinity using Hanna HI84531-01 alkalinity titrator and Lachart 8700 Flow injection analyzer. Other parameters (pCO 2 , saturation states for calcite (Ωcalc) and aragonite (Ωar)) were calculated using pH, total alkalinity, temperature and salinity using CO 2 sys [15,16]. 

The net coral calcification was measured using the 45 Ca technique [14]. All aquaria were spiked with 45 CaCl 2 (with the activity of 50 Bqml −1 ) for 72-h. After exposure, each sample was immersed for 30 s in 1 L of filtered seawater, then rinsed five times with 5 mL of ice-cold glycine.

documents.snippet: In terms of coral concrete preparation, there has been fundamental agreement that the special characteristics, such as large specific surface area and abundant surface porosity, would impose an extra cement dosage of about 30-40% when ensuring the same strength grade of coral concrete as conventional cement concrete [4]. On this basis, the object of subsequent experiments was to explore the variation in compressive strength and destroy the form of coral concrete with increasing cement dosage. As compiled in Table 11, the main construction ingredients comprised water, cement, coral debris particles, pre-wetting coral parent rock particles and a water-reducing admixture. Technically, cement dosage was applied by more than 500 kg/m 3 to obtain the strength grade C30 of coral concrete similar to conventional cement concrete. Last but not least, the particle proportion of coral debris to parent rock was ensured as high as 3:2 to promote the particle grade of coral aggregates (d < 19 mm), increase concrete mobility during mixing and strengthen the compressive strength of coral concrete. Another noteworthy point was that the parent rock particle was pre-wetted to satisfy its outstanding water absorbency. On the one hand, it is more convenient to determine the consistent water usage for both categories of coral aggregates during mixing. On the other hand, more water volume was prepared for supporting secondary hydration reactions and increasing the long-term concrete compressive strength. As illustrated in Figure 12, the compressive strength of coral concrete was initially in direct proportion to cement dosage; subsequently, the gradient of strength to dosage tended to decrease when cement dosage was more than 700 kg/m 3 . documents.title: Modelling coral calcification accounting for the impacts of coral bleaching and ocean acidification
documents.snippet:
Coral reefs are primarily composed of aragonite, a metastable crystal form of CaCO 3 produced by hermatypic corals, with an orthorhombic system of acicular crystals. Calcification rates are commonly related to the aragonite saturation state, which is a measure of the inorganic solution equilibrium between solid aragonite and calcium and carbonate ions in solution. The dependence of calcification rate on the seawater carbonate system has been investigated (Erez et al., 2011;Pandolfi et al., 2011;Schneider and Erez, 2006;Putron et al., 2010;Shamberger et al., 2011;Jokiel et al., 2014), but a full understanding of the process is yet to be achieved. Experiments have shown that corals ingest seawater and are able to manipulate its carbonate chemistry within the subcalicoblastic medium to up-regulate the aragonite saturation state well above the surrounding seawater to enhance the precipitation of aragonite crystals (Al-Horani, 2005;Venn et al., 2013). Recent evidence indicates that, rather than the decrease in aragonite saturation states, it could be change in external seawater pH due to ocean acidification that disrupts the pH balance in the underlying calcifying tissue (calicoblastic epithelium) of reef-building corals, which in turn reduces the rate of calcification (Venn et al., 2013). This is consistent with models for calcification that treat the flux of protons from photosynthesis, calcification and exchange with external seawater in detail (e.g. Jokiel , 2011). 

Our model employs an empirical relationship to describe how coral calcification relates to the carbonate chemistry of seawater on medium-to long-term timescales (weeks to annual increments of growth on decadal to centennial timescales). The model is not designed to capture diurnal changes, reef-scale hydrodynamics, boundary layers, biochemical pathways, etc. Instead it aims to describe the changes in "baseline" calcification by aggregating as many observational data as possible.
